articles.title: Employees cannot be forced to retire early without consent, Supreme Court says
articles.summary: The Supreme Court (SC) has ruled that employees cannot be retired before the compulsory retirement age of 65 without their clear and voluntary consent.

blocks.text: Published October 27, 2026 6:05pm
The Supreme Court (SC) has ruled that employees cannot be retired before the compulsory retirement age of 65 without their clear and voluntary consent.
In a 22-page decision, the SC’s First Division affirmed that under the Labor Code, an employee may opt to retire upon reaching 60 years old, but compulsory retirement remains set at 65.

“The Labor Code permits employers and employees to fix the applicable retirement age at below 60 years. Absent such an agreement, the retirement age shall be that fixed by law, and the above-cited law mandates that the compulsory retirement age is 65 years, while the minimum age for optional retirement is set at 60 years,” the SC said.

According to court records, petitioner Rodolfo C. Ondevilla was illegally dismissed by his employer, Colegio de San Juan de Letran - Laguna, when his appointment was treated as expired after he turned 60 years old.
The Labor Arbiter and the National Labor Relations Commission both ruled in Ondevilla’s favor, and the Court of Appeals (CA) likewise affirmed that he was illegally dismissed.

While the CA noted that Ondevilla had agreed to retire effective July 31, 2020, based on a letter sent to his employer, the high court affirmed his illegal dismissal because the school had denied his preferred retirement terms.

The SC emphasized that an optional retirement plan must be grounded on a mutual and voluntary agreement, with the employee freely and expressly consenting without pressure or coercion, as accepting optional retirement entails waiving the right to security of tenure.
“Considering that CSJL denied Ondevilla's preference to retire on July 31, 2020, he is deemed to have been illegally dismissed from employment,” the court said.

The Colegio de San Juan de Letran - Laguna was then ordered to pay Ondevilla full backwages from August 29, 2019 until August 29, 2024. He was also declared entitled to separation pay instead of reinstatement.
Furthermore, the SC awarded him retirement benefits covering his period of employment from June 16, 2004, until August 29, 2024, when he reached the mandatory retirement age of 65.
“The total monetary award shall earn legal interest at the rate of 6% per annum from August 29, 2019 until fully paid,” the decision read.
The decision was penned by Associate Justice Ramon Paul L. Hernando and promulgated in June 2026 and posted on social media on October 27, 2026. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Officials’ actions on unprogrammed funds presumed valid — Supreme Court justice
articles.summary: Public officials involved in the allocation and increase of unprogrammed funds cannot be held personally liable, as their actions carry the presumption of regularity, Supreme Court Associate Justice…

blocks.text: October 27, 2026 | 6:02pm
This file photo shows the seal of the Supreme Court.
Philstar.com / EC Toledo

MANILA, Philippines — Public officials involved in the allocation and increase of unprogrammed funds cannot be held personally liable, as their actions carry the presumption of regularity, Supreme Court Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda said.

During the interviews for the chief justice position on Monday, October 26, Zalameda, citing the high court’s ruling striking down provisions of the 2024, 2025 and 2026 General Appropriations Acts, said that because unprogrammed appropriations are not unconstitutional per se, the actions of the officials are presumed to be in good faith.
“When you say it is constitutional, I don't think the public officers may be held liable for such act, for act which is declared constitutional,” Zalameda said.

“Aside from that, there is presumption of regularity on the part of these public officials and all their acts are considered valid until such acts are declared invalid and they have the presumption of regularity,” he added.

During the interview, Zalameda also explained that under the constitutional principle of separation of powers, the executive, legislative and judicial branches operate with distinct and equal functions, bounded only by specific constitutional limitations.
He explained that unless a branch exceeds these limitations or commits a grave abuse of discretion, which falls under the court's expanded judicial review, the judiciary cannot intervene.

“Otherwise, these functions relating to the wisdom the different branches of the government specifically the executive and the legislative branches are policy wisdom, policy matters which cannot be included into by this court,” Zalameda said.

The Supreme Court, in its ruling on October 7, declared unconstitutional provisions of the 2024, 2025 and 2026 General Appropriations Acts concerning unauthorized congressional increases in unprogrammed funds and specific special accounts.
The high court emphasized that unprogrammed appropriations are not unconstitutional per se, as long as they comply with specific conditions.

articles.title: Yukon photographer captures footage of caribou carrying dead rival in its antlers
articles.summary: WARNING: This story contains graphic images of wildlife. Wildlife photographer Peter Mather said he was “shocked” to find a pair of bull caribou with antlers locked together, one of them dead, in the…

image.caption: In early October, photographer Peter Mather captured a bull caribou with his antlers locked with another, dead bull caribou south of Whitehorse. (Submitted by Peter Mather)

blocks.text: North

WARNING: This story contains graphic images of wildlife. Wildlife photographer Peter Mather said he was “shocked” to find a pair of bull caribou with antlers locked together, one of them dead, in the mountains south of Whitehorse earlier this month. He captured what happened as other wildlife fed off the carcass, still attached to the other bull.
Peter Mather was filming caribou rut south of Whitehorse when he found them
WARNING: This story contains graphic images of wildlife.
Earlier this month, Yukon-based wildlife photographer Peter Mather was on assignment south of Whitehorse to film caribou when he noticed a bear acting unusually aggressive.
“It was huffing and puffing and making noises and we had to scare it off,” Mather said.
Then, another bear came through.
Yukon photographer captures caribou carrying remains after antler entanglement
“When I saw that second bear there, I’m like ‘Oh, there’s probably some sort of dead caribou up there’,” Mather said.
He sent a drone up to see what was happening.
“I was just shocked to see … there’s two caribou with their antlers locked together, and one of them is dead,” he said.
He said he watched a bear nearby try to attack the caribou, but the surviving bull would scare the bear off.
Mather captured a variety of wildlife as they fed on the carcass of the dead bull caribou. Here, a bear and a conspiracy of ravens are seen. (Submitted by Peter Mather)
Mather said he watched this bull caribou for days.
“Over the four days that [dead] caribou disappeared,” Mather said.
“There were foxes … ravens, golden eagles were eating it for four days."
He said on the last day, a pack of wolves arrived at the scene. He believes they got much of the last of the carcass.
“In some ways, [they] kind of freed up this other caribou who could kind of walk away at the end, with two heads,” Mather said.
At one point, a fox stopped by for a meal from the dead caribou. (Submitted by Peter Mather)
Locking antlers not unheard of
Mather said after the wolves arrived and feasted, the living caribou disappeared, and he couldn’t find it.
His work was to record the rut, mating season for caribou that often involve the males fighting one another, with the Southern Lakes Caribou Recovery Team and the Kwanlin Dün First Nation.
Lars Jessup, a biologist with the Southern Lakes Caribou Recovery Project, said this incident happened in a season where bull caribou are especially vulnerable.
“The rut season is the most dangerous time of year for bull caribou … they work really hard in the rut and the predators are usually around during the rut.”
He said bulls locking antlers is somewhat common, describing finding skulls and skeletons of caribou with locked antlers in the past.
“It’s probably more common that when that happens that they both die, not that one of them would live,” Jessup said, calling the living caribou “lucky.”
His time with the extra weight is also coming to an end, Jessup said.
“If he makes it another month or so, he’s likely to drop those antlers and lose the extra weight, and should be fine through winter,” Jessup said.
“By the time people usually see them down the mountains in and around Christmas time … the bulls are usually bald.”
Eventually, other animals managed to free the surviving caribou from having to carry the extra weight of another bull. (Submitted by Peter Mather)
A metaphor for the herd's resiliency
This particular caribou is part of the Ibex herd, Jessup said, one of four caribou herds that make up the southern lakes caribou herds.
It is protected by the southern lakes caribou recovery project, which has continued for more than 30 years.
“The herds have done really well to recover over the last three decades, through all kinds of hard work and effort,” Jessup said.
However, he said there were concerns the natural ebb and flow of the caribou population was in an ebb, as they haven’t seen many calves in the last five years.
For Mather, the photographer, the footage he captured of that one caribou surviving, gives him some hope.
“For me, it’s like a metaphor for the whole herd, that he’s just resilient, just a really, really resilient caribou.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Julia Parrish is a digital associate producer at CBC North in Yellowknife. You can reach her at julia.parrish@cbc.ca
With files from Leonard Linklater

articles.title: Nopes to the nine? Blue walls? Five takeaways from Alberta's referendum results
articles.summary: A majority of provincial ridings rejected most of Danielle Smith's ballot questions.

image.caption: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith hoped to sweep her nine referendum questions on immigration and constitutional reform, but voters had different ideas, rejecting four of her ballot measures. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Calgary·Analysis
A majority of provincial ridings rejected most of Danielle Smith's ballot questions.
Most provincial ridings rejected most of Danielle Smith's ballot questions
The “strong mandates” that Premier Danielle Smith requested on her nine referendum questions never materialized.
But aside from soft support, there might be another reason Smith is expressing reluctance to act quickly, even on the immigration questions where she won a majority.
Consider that Smith’s own government mandate isn’t derived from the popular vote — it’s based on prevailing in a majority of Alberta’s 87 seats.
And sifting through the riding results from all the referendum questions, some apparent political signals emerge.
Here are some takeaways:
Ridings say no to seven of nine

Smith has signalled she’ll act most quickly on the ballot measure that got the most support — Question 5, to require proof of Canadian citizenship when voting in provincial elections (58 per cent support).
She’s also intent to continue wresting from Ottawa more provincial control over immigration to Alberta, as Question 1 suggested (55 per cent support).

The victory margins were tighter on Questions 2, 3 and 4, to variously restrict social services and financial supports for temporary residents. But on each of those questions, a slight majority of ridings went no — meaning that while four of Smith’s questions failed in terms of total vote, seven of nine would have lost if this was a riding-by-riding contest.
Edmonton was almost uniformly opposed to those temporary resident questions, and only six Calgary ridings were supportive of them.

Twelve Calgary ridings had gone UCP in the last election, which suggests that several parts of Calgary that supported Smith in the 2023 election weren’t on board with her ideas on who should or shouldn’t get fully covered health and education.
Constitutionally blocked
The per-riding results on Question 1 (48 yes, 39 no) roughly tracked the seat math after the last provincial election (48 UCP, 39 NDP).
But on Questions 6 to 9, Smith would have been on the wrong end of the sort of landslides that former premiers Ralph Klein and Jason Kenney enjoyed, had this referendum been settled riding by riding.

More than two-thirds of ridings voted no to Question 8 on opting out of federal social service programs, the most lopsided of the constitutional ballot measures. But in all of them, no was the popular choice in more than 50 constituencies.
Not a single riding in Edmonton or Calgary said yes to a single one of the constitutional questions.
Rural Alberta, however, stayed loyal to Smith’s push for more provincial powers and to tilt Canada’s Constitution in favour of Alberta.
Blue wall, orange wall
Premier Smith asked voters to vote yes on all nine questions that didn’t threaten national unity; NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi was effectively part of the “no to the nine” campaign.
According to Elections Alberta, 24 ridings voted no down the line, while 27 voted yes to all of them.

items: Alberta referendum tallies reveal rural-urban divide on ‘the 9’

blocks.text: What went all the UCP government’s way? Ridings that solidly backed the party in 2023, including all predominantly rural or small-town seats, as well as the seats that include Grande Prairie, Medicine Hat and Fort McMurray.

The all-no seats? Most of them were in Edmonton, some in inner-city Calgary and its northeast, as well as St. Albert — a seat which has gone NDP in the last three elections — and Banff-Kananaskis, which has swung back and forth between UCP and NDP.
Swing ridings?
While a majority of ridings in Alberta went either solidly yes or solidly no, that still leaves 36 provincial constituencies where voters were choosier about how they marked their referendum ballots.
Which seats were running hot and cold on Smith’s plea for referendum support, and might wind up being hotly contested in next year’s election?

Of Calgary’s 26 ridings, 18 of them delivered a mixed yes-and-no verdict on the referendum questions. That includes a handful of NDP-held seats — as well as all the UCP-held seats in the province's largest city.

Calgary has become swing city in Alberta provincial politics, and offered the greatest mix of yes and no verdicts on the premier's referendum questions, compared to the solidly no-leaning Edmonton and yes-leaning other areas of the province. (CBC)
A few suburban Edmonton constituencies broke up the capital’s preference for no with yes majorities on Question 5.

Most of the ridings that surround Edmonton — known politically as the doughnut — swung between yes and no, including NDP-held Sherwood Park, as well as UCP-controlled Spruce Grove-Stony Plain, Strathcona-Sherwood Park, Morinville-St. Albert and Leduc-Beaumont.
Lethbridge’s two seats were a mixed bag too, as they have been politically in the last few elections.

Voters in Alberta’s other two cities of around 100,000 people — Red Deer and rapidly growing Airdrie — have been more consistently UCP in recent votes. But in all four of those cities’ ridings, voters defied Smith’s bid for a clean sweep by voting against Question 8 (and Question 9, in Airdrie-Cochrane).
Calgary-Shaw went orange, but…
Nenshi’s NDP managed to take away a formerly deep-blue suburban seat in September, in the Calgary-Shaw byelection.
The much-watched riding voted yes to all immigration questions last week, but no to all constitutional questions.
Newly elected Calgary-Shaw MLA Kyle Campbell, left, celebrates his byelection victory with NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi. (CBC News)
That more closely resembles voting patterns in other UCP ridings like Calgary-Peigan, Calgary-South East and Calgary-Hays.

However, it’s striking which seat featured a voting result more similar to NDP-held districts: Calgary-West, which voted yes to Question 5 on citizenship markers, but no to the rest. That seat has been held by Deputy Premier Mike Ellis since 2015.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jason Markusoff is a CBC producer and writer. He analyzes what's happening — and what isn't happening, but probably should be — in Calgary, in Alberta and sometimes farther afield. He's covered Alberta for more than two decades, previously reporting for Maclean's magazine, Calgary Herald and Edmonton Journal. He appears regularly on Power and Politics, West of Centre and various other CBC current affairs shows. Reach him at jason.markusoff@cbc.ca

articles.title: Winnipegger facing extradition over COVID relief fraud, money laundering allegations
articles.summary: A Winnipeg man is facing extradition after U.S. authorities accused him of defrauding a pandemic-era relief program of hundreds of thousands of dollars.

image.caption: Ajay Singh of Winnipeg is facing extradition to the U.S. on allegations he was involved in a scheme to defraud a COVID-19 relief program in that country. (Realtor.ca)

blocks.text: Manitoba
A Winnipeg man is facing extradition after U.S. authorities accused him of defrauding a pandemic-era relief program of hundreds of thousands of dollars.
Ajay Singh, 46, used fake payroll numbers for forgivable loans through pandemic-era program, U.S. says

Ajay Singh, a 46-year-old Canadian citizen, was arrested last December on allegations he was part of a bank fraud and money laundering scheme to get funds meant to help small businesses pay workers during the COVID-19 pandemic.

U.S. officials accused Singh of using inflated or fake payroll numbers to successfully apply for more than $11.5 million US in forgivable loans, according to an extradition request submitted by the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Wisconsin.
The lender, Wells Fargo, was able to recover most of the money, but more than $600,000 US was unaccounted for, the document said.
The request did not mention any specific charges Singh — also known as Ajay Singh Kalkat — would face in the U.S. A final decision on whether he should be extradited is pending.

The man had asked courts to stop the proceedings, arguing Canadian authorities violated his Charter rights by issuing an arrest warrant without knowing what he would be charged with. A Manitoba Court of King's Bench judge dismissed that application in September.
The extradition request "contained detailed descriptions of the conduct underlying these allegations, including the names of witnesses and documents," Justice Ami Kotler wrote in the decision.

"This does not mean that Mr. Singh is not entitled to know what charges he is facing in the United States," Kotler said. "But the failure to identify these charges in the warrant application did not, in my view, represent a violation of Mr. Singh's [Charter] rights."

items: 3rd person charged in alleged $11M scheme to defraud Ontario COVID-19 relief fund

blocks.text: The U.S. extradition request said Singh applied to the federal COVID Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) 19 times through three Wisconsin-based companies between 2020 and 2021: Aikam Logistics, AK Hunt Capital Finance LLC and AK Hunt Ltd.
Four of the applications were approved, the document said.

Trucking company Aikam Logistics was granted a $301,882 US loan in 2020 for payroll purposes, with Singh submitting documents that said it had 10 employees. U.S. authorities allege only about $5,000 US appeared to have been spent on items that could possibly be business related.
A year later, Singh submitted another loan application for Aikam, with documents saying the company had 97 employees, the extradition request said. Aikam received a loan for $997,000 US.
Some companies 'existed only on paper,' officials say
Officials pointed to inconsistencies in the number of employees Singh reported to have in 2020 compared with 2021.
The U.S. document also contains allegations the two other companies owned by Singh "existed only on paper in that they did not pay employees or earn revenue."
AK Hunt received a $301,882 US loan based on an application saying it had nine employees in 2020.
AK Hunt Capital Finance LLC. received a $9,975,000 US loan in 2021. The application said the company had 497 employees.
The documents say a witness would be able to testify in court that the office listed as the address for AK Hunt Capital Finance was not large enough to host that many employees.
The witness could say Singh was renting the space for about half a year, paying $450 US a month, officials said.

items: Ex-bureaucrat accused of embezzling COVID-19 funds from Ontario government now facing criminal charges

blocks.text: Wells Fargo began closing business accounts linked to those companies after approving the $9.9-million US loan in March 2021. The document said several identical applications had previously been rejected.
The document said Singh sent a letter to the bank agreeing to reverse the last loan in April 2021 after being interviewed by a Wells Fargo investigator.
"It has come to my attention that the PPP funds should not be used for the purposes I intended," the letter said.
Singh did not address the other loans that were approved, U.S. officials said.
Thousands spent on jewelry, document says

The extradition request said an Internal Revenue Service investigator would be able to give testimony about several transactions that took place after each of the loans was granted, including transfers to broker and personal accounts in multiple banks, as well as cashier cheque purchases.
The investigator had also traced about $15,000 US of the money in jewelry purchases for Singh's wife, the document said.
Kotler said in the September decision the allegations outlined in the U.S. request would have carried a maximum jail sentence of 14 years under Canada's Criminal Code.
An RCMP officer said in an affidavit it was in the public interest to issue the arrest warrant.
Singh was granted bail under several conditions in December, including that he surrender his passport to police.
He was also barred from having sole authority for financial transactions or loans as part of his employment.
The inspector general for the U.S. Small Business Administration estimated more than $200 billion US in COVID-19 aid was potentially fraudulent, including $64 billion US in PPP loan funds.
CBC News tried to contact Singh, but he was not immediately available.
The United States Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Wisconsin declined to comment.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Arturo Chang is a reporter with CBC Manitoba. Before that, he worked for CBC P.E.I. and BNN Bloomberg. You can reach him at arturo.chang@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Are Canadian conservatives ditching the fringe?
articles.summary: The B.C. Conservatives were falling apart just last month. Then they united and won the election in a landslide. What happened? And what can other conservative parties learn?

image.caption: B.C. Conservative interim Leader Lorne Doerkson celebrates on stage during provincial election night in Vancouver, on Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026.THE CANADIAN PRESS/Ethan Cairns (THE CANADIAN PRESS)

blocks.text: Front Burner
The B.C. Conservatives were falling apart just last month. Then they united and won the election in a landslide. What happened? And what can other conservative parties learn?
LISTEN | FRONT BURNER:
Front Burner26:15Are Canadian conservatives ditching the fringe?

At the end of September the B.C. Conservative party had imploded. Today, they are set to run the province. It's a stunning reversal of political fortune for a party that had been torn apart by infighting and resignations before a snap election call by the NDP.

The whole situation raises a tonne of interesting questions. Was this a triumph of one particular brand of conservatism over another? Or just a rejection of the NDP? Are there lessons here for Danielle Smith in Alberta and the struggling federal Conservatives?

articles.title: Malacañang: Nothing wrong with budget insertions as long as used properly
articles.summary: Malacañang responded to a watchdog's finding that Ilocos Norte 1st district had the highest public work insertions in the proposed 2027 budget.

blocks.text: Published October 27, 2026 5:59pm

Malacañang on Tuesday said that budget “insertions” only become problematic if they go into politicians' pockets, after a watchdog found that Ilocos Norte 1st district had the highest insertions for public works projects in the proposed House General Appropriations Bill (GAB), amounting to P4.37 billion.
The district is represented by President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr.'s son, House Majority Leader Sandro Marcos.

“Kung ang mga proyekto naman ng isang congressman ay maayos at ang pondong ilalaan dito ay magagamit nang tama, sino ba naman ang dapat na humadlang kung ang pondong ito ay sasapat naman para mapaganda ang isang distrito?” Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro said in a press briefing in Cagayan de Oro City when asked to comment on the People's Budget Coalition's report.
(If a congressman’s projects are justifiable and the allocated funds for such would be properly used to improve the district, then why should we stand in the way?)
“Mahirap po kasi na kumukuha ng pondo, ‘yun pala hindi naman nagagamit sa distrito,” she added.
(What’s problematic is when funds are given only for them not to be used for the district.)
The Palace official said she is not specifically referring to the younger Marcos, but all congressmen in general.
She stressed that there are no problems with such insertions as long as they are used for the welfare of the constituents.

“Kahit sino pang congressman 'yan, kung ang pondo na nailaan sa kanyang distrito ay tama ang paggamit---walang ghost projects, walang substandard na mga materials na ginamit sa mga proyekto---hindi po ito po magkakaroon ng problema,” Castro said.
(Regardless of who the congressman is, as long as the funds allocated to their district are used properly—with no ghost projects and no substandard materials—there shouldn’t be any problem.)
“Dahil ang insertion ay hindi po ito generally masama. Nagiging masama lang ang insertion kung ang pera ay i-insert sa bulsa ng pulitiko. ‘Yun ang masama,” she added.
(An insertion is not inherently bad. It only becomes problematic when the funds are inserted into a politician’s own pocket. That is what’s wrong.)
The People's Budget Coalition (PBC) earlier said it found "red flags" amounting to over P1 trillion in allocations in the proposed P7.2 trillion national budget for fiscal year 2027.
These reportedly covered various types of “pork” or discretionary funds under the House-approved GAB

“Lampas P1 trilyong red flags ang nakita namin sa 2027 budget—P210 billion sa soft pork sa anyo ng patronage-driven ayuda, P695 billion sa hard pork, which is politicized infrastructure, and P112 billion po sa shadow pork o ‘yung unprogrammed appropriations,” PBC co-convenor AJ Montesa said in a budget briefing at the Senate on Monday.

(We identified over P1 trillion worth of ‘red flags’ under the 2027 budget—P210 billion of which was ‘soft pork’ in the form of patronage-driven financial assistance; P695 billion in ‘hard pork,’ which consists of politicized infrastructure projects; and P112 billion in ‘shadow pork,’ or unprogrammed appropriations.)

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian, in response, said that Congress could make adjustments in the proposed budget with a valid basis. Regardless, he said the Senate would assess if such amendments made by the House were necessary. — BM, GMA News
Follow facebook.com/gmanewsonline for real-time news and developments in the Philippines and around the world.

articles.title: Serbia’s student movement toppled a political giant. Can it now govern the country?
articles.summary: Tens of thousands of people take to the streets across the country to celebrate after Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat late on October 25 in a historic poll that capped two years of peaceful…

blocks.text: BELGRADE, Serbia – By unseating longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic in Sunday’s election on October 25, Serbia’s student protest movement did what demonstrators in other European capitals can only dream of. Now, though, comes the gritty business of governing — something neither the students nor their handpicked candidates have any experience of.

Tens of thousands of people took to the streets across the country to celebrate when Vucic conceded defeat late on Sunday in a historic poll that capped two years of peaceful anti-government protests.

But as the jubilant crowd lit flares and fireworks, sang and danced, questions lingered: who will emerge from this leaderless movement as prime minister, what exactly will their policies be, and can a bunch of political unknowns with no previous affiliation stick together to shore up the economy, root out graft and juggle complex international relations?
The answers will determine the political stability of Serbia, the largest economy in the Western Balkans, and its relations with China, Russia, and its largest trading partner, the European Union.

The students’ victory “is likely to trigger broad institutional and policy changes centered on anti-corruption, the rule of law, and better public services. However, bureaucratic resistance to reforms and the movement’s limited governing experience could make the transition challenging,” Teneo Global Research said in a report on Monday, October 26.

The protest movement began after 16 people died when a railway station canopy collapsed in the northern city of Novi Sad in 2024, and the student-led demonstrations called for accountability and an end to corruption.
Despite not having a figurehead, the students won widespread support before choosing 250 academics, lawyers, doctors, actors, farmers and musicians to represent them in the election.
The movement and some of the top candidates on its list have given some idea of what it stands for, promising a domestic anti-corruption program centered on institutional overhauls.

It does not recognise Kosovo, Serbia’s former southern province which declared independence in 2008, but wants to hold a referendum on Serbia’s accession to the EU, with which relations have frayed in recent years.

Prominent figures include the head of the students’ candidate list, cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, former central bank governor Dejan Soskic and Radomir Sajcic, a professor at Belgrade University, who spoke on behalf of the students following their victory. But there is no certainty that any of them will hold a ministerial post, and it remains to be seen whether the candidates can form a cohesive government that can agree on policy long enough to use their comfortable parliamentary majority to enact change.
“(The student movement created) such a shift in Serbia’s culture; we will just have to see if it lasts,” said Katarina Popovic, also a professor at the University of Belgrade.
“We just hope that there are big goals that can keep them together long enough to deconstruct the system.”
Under Serbia’s constitution, the students’ candidates have 90 days to form a government once parliament is convened after the announcement of final results by the state election commission.

Time matters, especially with a budget to pass before year-end amid growing public and private debt levels, while any attempt to end corruption will require an overhaul of the police and intelligence services and judicial reform.
State institutions require “detoxification” after 14 years of Vucic, said Bozo Prelevic, a Belgrade-based lawyer and former co-minister of the interior.
Prelevic warned that Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), will pose a strong opposition, and that the new government would have to fight its corner.
Vucic and the SNS repeatedly denied accusations of repression and corruption.
In Russia, Serbia’s traditional ally and principal supplier of natural gas, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov praised Vucic, but stopped short of congratulating the students.

“We respect Russia both as a great power and as our historically important partner and, in many cases, protector,” Student List representative Jovo Bakic, a sociologist and a university lecturer, told Russia’s RT Balkan TV, adding that there would be no change in Serbia’s foreign policy towards Russia, including not introducing sanctions against Moscow.
Also closely watching is Ukraine, which has been an indirect beneficiary of Serbian weapons in its fight to repel Russia’s four-year-long invasion.
European officials congratulated the students and said they stood ready to help the country in its fight against corruption.

“I am sure (the Student List) will find a way, just as they have so far, to choose someone capable of governing — someone who will have the privilege, but also the immense responsibility, to lead Serbia through these reforms,” said Savo Manojlovic of the student-friendly Move-Change movement. – Rappler.com

blocks.text: October 27, 2026
Some 5% of Germany potentially suitable for long-term nuclear waste storage

blocks.caption: Germany is currently searching for a suitable location to store its nuclear waste Image: Cigdem Simsek/Zoonar/picture alliance

blocks.text: The German agency responsible for finding a final repository for nuclear waste (BGE) has eliminated five states from its search.
Berlin, Hesse, Rhineland-Palatinate, Saxony and Saarland were deemed unsuitable for long-term radioactive waste storage.

In a report issued Tuesday, the BGE said it had limited its search to 5% of Germany, down from 25% in 2025. The federal agency aims to suggest suitable locations for final evaluation by the end of 2027.
Regions in northern, northwestern, southern and eastern Germany remain under consideration as locations for final storage facilities.
Germany's nuclear waste is currently stored in 16 above-ground interim storage facilities.

The BGE assessments evaluate regions' geological conditions and their ability to safely contain highly radioactive material. Granite, salt, and clay are generally considered potentially suitable types of rock and areas with damaged or compromised subsurface conditions, places with mines or volcanos have been active, are not eligible as final disposal sites.

Germany needs to find a repository for approximately 27,000 cubic meters of highly radioactive nuclear waste generated over more than 60 years of nuclear power generation. The site is expected to ensure safety for 1 million years. The last German nuclear power plants were decommissioned in April 2023.
BGE said its goal remains finding the site that offers the highest level of safety for highly radioactive waste.
The agency's recommendations, however, are not legally binding and it will be up to German lawmakers to determine the final disposal site.

articles.title: [In This Economy] Pagsadsad ng piso: Ano ang puwedeng gawin?
articles.summary: Sa ngayon, makatutulong ang pagplano ng bayarin at pag-iwas sa padalos-dalos na financial decisions. Pero may pananagutan din ang gobyerno na gawing mas matatag ang ekonomiya.

blocks.text: Mabilis ang pagsadsad ng piso kontra dolyar sa mga nakalipas na araw. Ngayong Martes, Oktubre 27, nagsara ang palitan sa P64.17 kada dolyar, isang bagong record low.

Para sa mga pamilyang hirap nang pagkasyahin ang kita, dagdag na pangamba ito sa presyo ng mga bilihin. Kahit wala ka kasing hawak na dolyar, puwede mong maramdaman ang pagsadsad ng piso sa pamamalengke, pagpapagasolina, at pagbili ng LPG.

Mas maraming piso na kasi ang kailangan para bumili ng parehong dami ng dolyar. At dahil dolyar ang pambayad sa maraming inaangkat o iniimport, puwedeng tumaas ang gastos sa langis, pagkain, at iba’t ibang sangkap o kagamitan na ginagamit ng mga negosyo.

Pero hindi awtomatikong pantay ang paghina ng piso sa itataas ng lahat ng presyo. Nakadepende iyon sa presyo sa world market, dami ng lumang imbentaryo, at kung gaano kalaking dagdag-gastos ang kayang saluhin ng negosyo.
Ano ang magagawa ng ordinaryong Pilipino? May ilang praktikal na hakbang.

I-prioritize ang mga gastusing mahirap takasan: pagkain, pamasahe, upa, gamot, at baon ng mga bata. Kung kaya, ilista ang gastos sa loob ng isang linggo para makita kung alin sa mga ito ang tumataas at saan kailangang magdagdag ng pondo.

Halimbawa, kung P200 ang budget sa pagkain bawat araw at naging P220 ang parehong binibili, dagdag na P600 iyon sa loob ng 30 araw. Hindi ibig sabihing exchange rate lang ang dahilan ng pagtaas na ito. Pero malaking bagay kasi sa pamilya ang kahit maliit na dagdag kada araw.

Sa palengke o grocery, ikumpara ang presyo kada kilo, litro, o gramo. Maaaring mas mura kada gramo ang malaking pakete kaysa sachet. Pero sulit lang iyon kung may perang pambili, talagang magagamit ang laman, at hindi masasakripisyo ang ibang pangangailangan.

Kung praktikal, puwede ring maghati ang magkakamag-anak o magkakapitbahay sa pagbili ng bigas o ibang produktong mas mura kapag maramihan. Isama rin sa kuwenta ang pamasahe at delivery. Walang matitipid kung mas mahal ang biyahe kumpara sa bawas-presyo, o kung masisira lang ang sobrang pagkain.
Iwasan ding mangutang nang mahal para lang makabili nang maramihan. Dapat hindi rin humantong ang pagtitipid sa paglaktaw ng pagkain o pag-inom ng gamot.
Sa pamasahe, puwedeng pagsabayin ang mga lakad kung kaya. Pero hindi lahat ay may parehong ruta o oras ng trabaho.
Para sa mga may karinderya, puwedeng planuhin ang pagluluto para masulit ang LPG at mabawasan ang tirang pagkain, nang hindi isinasantabi ang kalinisan at ligtas na pag-iimbak ng pagkain.

Maraming pamilya ang ginagawa na ang lahat ng ito. Kaya hindi sapat ang paulit-ulit na payong “magtipid.” Sa kalaunan, kailangang mapunta rin ang mga diskusyon sa pagiging sapat ng kita ng mga manggagawa, at kung anong mga serbisyo ng gobyerno ang maaaring magpababa sa gastos araw-araw.

blocks.caption: [In This Economy] Investment options sa panahon ng mataas na inflation

blocks.text: Para sa pamilyang may OFW, maaaring may dagdag na piso mula sa remittances o padala. Halimbawa, ang $200 ay P12,000 sa palitang P60 kada dolyar at P12,800 sa P64. Dagdag na P800 rin iyon, at least bago ibawas ang fees.

Pero maaaring mas mahal na rin ang bigas, pamasahe, at iba pang binabayaran ng pamilya. Dahil dito, kailangang ikumpara ang halagang aktuwal na matatanggap matapos ang lahat ng fees. Huwag ipagpaliban ang padalang kailangan na sa pagkain o gamot dahil lang umaasang mas gaganda pa ang palitan.

Kung may natira, puwedeng unahin ang nalalapit na bills o bawasan ang utang na mataas ang interes. Huwag lang ipang-shopping ang buong diperensya sa palitan. Para sa mga OFWs, mag-usap muna tungkol sa budget bago sila mag-commit sa pagpapadala ng mas malaking remittances.

Para sa mga sari-sari store, balikan ang presyo ng supplier bago muling mag-stock. Ihiwalay ang puhunan sa perang pambahay hangga’t kaya. Kung tumaas ang presyo ng kapalit na paninda, maaaring hindi sapat ang dating nakalaang puhunan kahit naibenta na ang lahat ng lumang stock.

Sa mga karinderya naman, kuwentahin ulit ang gastos sa mga sangkap, LPG, at lalagyan. Puwedeng magbawas ng pagkaing madalas matira o baguhin ang menu ayon sa presyong afford ng mga suki. Hindi rin magandang solusyon ang biglang pagtaas ng presyo nang walang malinaw na kuwenta, dahil baka lalo lang humina ang benta.

Para sa jeepney driver o delivery rider, itala ang netong naiuuwi matapos ang gasolina, boundary kung mayroon, at ibang gastos. Kung kailangang magdagdag ng oras para maabot ang dating kita, mahalagang makita kung gaano talaga kalaki ang kinain ng dagdag-gastos.
Siyempre, may hangganan ang lahat ng payong ito. Walang household budget na kayang resolbahin ang pagdepende natin sa imported fuel o iba pang sanhi ng mataas na inflation.

May papel ang Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas sa pagpigil sa sobrang pagkabalisa ng merkado at pagkalat ng inflation. Halimbawa, maaari silang magbenta ng supply natin ng dolyar para awatin ang pagsadsad ng piso. Pero gumagamit ito ng bilyon-bilyong dolyar, kaya may hangganan ang pagtatanggol nila sa palitan.

May kapalit din ang kanilang pagtaas ng interest rates kamakailan: puwedeng mas mahal ang pautang at mas humina ang paggastos at investment. Delikado ito dahil ngayon pa lang ay sobrang hina na ng paglaki ng ating ekonomiya. Kailangang timbangin ang mga ito laban sa panganib ng patuloy na pagtaas ng presyo.

Samantala, dapat ihanda na ng gobyerno ang tulong sa mga pamilyang pinakatinatamaan ng mahal na pagkain at transportasyon, kasama ang mga driver at maliliit na negosyante. Kailangang malinaw din kung sino ang kuwalipikado at paano makakakuha, upang hindi umaasa sa padrino.
Sa paparating na Super El Niño, inaasahang lalong magpapataas ito sa presyo ng mga bilhin. Hindi puwedeng balde-balde lang ang solusyong maiaalok ng gobyerno.

Mahalaga rin ang maayos na paggamit ng pondo ng bayan. Ang perang nasasayang sa palpak na mga proyekto ay hindi nakadaragdag sa kakayahan nating gumawa ng produkto, maghatid ng serbisyo, o bawasan ang gastos ng negosyo. Ang problema, mahigit isang trilyong na insertions at pork barrel funds na naman ang gustong ilagay ng mga politiko sa 2027 budget. Juskopo.
Sa ngayon, makatutulong ang pagplano ng bayarin at pag-iwas sa padalos-dalos na financial decisions. Pero may pananagutan din ang gobyerno na gawing mas matatag ang ekonomiya.
Hindi puwedeng tayo lang parati ang nag-aadjust. – Rappler.com

Jan Carlo “JC” Punongbayan, PhD, is an associate professor at the University of the Philippines School of Economics. His professional experience includes the Securities and Exchange Commission, the World Bank Office in Manila, the Far Eastern University Public Policy Center, and the National Economic and Development Authority. JC writes a weekly economics column for Rappler. He is also co-founder of UsapangEcon.com and co-host of Usapang Econ Podcast.

His first book, False Nostalgia: The Marcos “Golden Age” Myths and How to Debunk Them, was published by Ateneo de Manila University Press in February 2023. His second book, Twin Plagues: How Duterte and COVID-19 Wrecked the Philippine Economy, was published by Penguin Random House SEA in June 2026. Follow him on Instagram (@jcpunongbayan).

articles.title: Nearly half of Davao Region students struggle to read, says EDCOM 2
articles.summary: Nearly half of students assessed in the Davao Region at the start of the school year in June were classified as struggling readers, according to a Department of Education assessment.

blocks.text: October 27, 2026 | 5:47pm
Students look for their room assignment as classes open for the new school year at an elementary school in Manila on June 8, 2026.
AFP / Jam Sta Rosa

MANILA, Philippines — Nearly half of students assessed in the Davao Region at the start of the school year in June were classified as struggling readers, according to a Department of Education assessment.
A congressional education commission shared its analysis of the findings Tuesday, October 27, as it called on local governments to help close the region's literacy gaps.

Citing DepEd's Comprehensive Rapid Literacy Assessment (CRLA), the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM 2) said 48% of learners in Region XI and 45 percent in Davao City fell into the test's two lowest reading levels at the beginning of school year 2026-2027.

Struggling readers refer to students classified as "emerging readers" — students who are still trying to master basic foundational literacy skills like recognizing letters, connecting sounds, and forming simple words.

DepEd's rapid literacy assessment splits emerging readers into two specific sublevels: "low emerging and high emerging." Under DepEd guidelines, students at the "low-emerging" level have limited mastery of letters and their sounds, while those at the "high-emerging" level recognize most letters but still struggle to decode words at their grade level.
Municipality- and city-level results from the previous school year show variations in reading skills.

For instance, in Talaingod, Davao del Norte, 49.6% of students in Grades 1 to 3, or 1,184 children, were still struggling readers in the end-of-year assessment in March, about twice the rate of any other municipality in the region.

"The learning crisis did not happen overnight, it has compounded over the years," EDCOM 2 Executive Director Karol Mark Yee said in a statement. "Every child who continues to struggle with reading needs timely support. Otherwise, they risk moving up to the next grade without fully understanding their lessons."
The Davao results appear to track with the overall nationwide data. EDCOM 2 said 45% of students assessed nationwide at the start of the current school year were struggling readers.

The data also shows reading proficiency further thinning out as students move up levels, from 30.52% in Grade 3 to 19.56% in Grade 6, 0.74% in Grade 10 and 0.40% in Grade 12, or roughly one in every 250 students in the final year of high school.

DepEd said in May that the number of struggling readers across all grade levels fell from 6.7 million at the start of school year 2025-2026 to 2.2 million by its end, which it credited to intensified learning recovery programs.
In September, the Philippines posted its best performance to date in reading, science and math, though it continues to fall below the global average.
All 10 school divisions with the highest shares of struggling readers at the start of the last school year were in Mindanao, according to EDCOM 2 in March.
EDCOM 2 has pressed local executives to take a larger role in basic education.
In March, it released a playbook to help mayors manage schooling in their towns, the same document that ranked school divisions by their share of struggling readers.

articles.title: UK officials discussing free movement with EU ahead of summit, says Reynolds
articles.summary: Business secretary says focus for November summit will be trade and youth mobility, but talks will also include ‘future options for relationship’

blocks.text: British officials have begun discussions with the EU about a long-term relationship that could include a return to free movement, the business secretary has said while promising the British people “are the boss” when it comes to what the UK will accept.

Jonathan Reynolds said the focus for British negotiations was the EU summit in November to seal an agreement to ease some trading restrictions and a youth mobility deal. But he said the prime minister, Andy Burnham, had made it clear he wanted to see a long-term and stable relationship with the bloc.

“They will be talking to them about what the future options for our relationship might be. But here and now, the focus should be on the summit and the tangible difference improvements we’re going to make,” he told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme.

He said the changes announced at the EU summit, including a food and drink deal and on emissions trading, would make a significant difference. But he added: “What the prime minister has also said, quite rightly, is we face a series of policy changes on the European side that will affect us, and we need to get as little uncertainty as possible.

“We need to have a way to resolve what our long-term relationship will be, and he is going to set that out after the summit. And he is going to be frank with the British people about what the trade-offs are.”

Reynolds said there had been “no assumptions made about the next stage after that. It’s the prime minister quite rightly saying he wants to set out to the British people what the options are to resolve some of the tensions that exist.”

He said no decision would be made without voters being given a say, without specifying whether this would be through a general election or a referendum. “No assumptions have been made on this. The British people are the people who will decide this. They’re the boss on this,” he said.
A number of backbenchers with heavily pro-Brexit seats in the north and Midlands are wary about reopening the arguments for free movement or rejoining the EU.

The Labour MP for Great Grimsby and Cleethorpes, Melanie Onn, was among those urging caution. “I am still not over the kind of very divisive debate that we had when we were leaving the EU post the referendum, and I don’t think that the scars have healed for many people around the country,” she told Today. “So I do think that this is an unnecessary conversation to be having at this time.”

The Reform UK leader, Nigel Farage, told the programme it would be “very, very poor indeed” to begin discussing freedom of movement. “Five months ago, Andy Burnham says to leave-voting Makerfield: ‘I’m not going to reopen these arguments.’ Two and a half years ago, a Labour government got a massive majority in parliament saying we will not be re-entering the single market, the customs union, or opening up the debate on the free movement of people,” he said.
“What I am saying is this: this prime minister has no mandate, and to hear that his officials are negotiating in Brussels already is really very, very poor indeed.”

Burnham made his plea for an “honest discussion” about freedom of movement in an interview with the Sunday Times, making clear that staying out of it would no longer be a red line in talks with the EU.

Burnham also shared his belief that rejoining the single market and accepting free movement could be done without the need for another referendum, if Labour put it in its manifesto. In contrast, he said fully rejoining would need another in-out poll.

The prime minister said: “Freedom of movement had very significant challenges associated with it and I spoke about them in my previous time in parliament. But, at the same time, it was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult [as now].

“Revolving-door migration where people would come and then go back is different. The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things.”

articles.title: Midas Marquez eyes to tap PDLs for SC's digitalization efforts
articles.summary: Supreme Court (SC) Associate Justice Midas Marquez is eyeing to tap persons deprived of liberty (PDLs) in the court's efforts to digitalize its non-sensitive records as part of their reformation and…

blocks.text: Published October 27, 2026 5:32pm

Supreme Court (SC) Associate Justice Midas Marquez is eyeing to tap persons deprived of liberty (PDLs) in the court's efforts to digitalize its non-sensitive records as part of their reformation and reintegration program.
This is one of the priorities laid down by Marquez during his interview with the Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) for the position of chief justice.
"I intend to continuously support, empower, and involve PDLs, more than just conducting the usual PDL Arts and Crafts Exhibition and Sale," he said.

"For their reformation and eventual reintegration, perhaps they can initially assist in realizing the Court's digitization transformation where they will be tasked with digitizing non-sensitive Judiciary-wide court records, and they will be provided with a corresponding stipend therefor," he added.
Marquez said that if appointed chief justice, he will build on the foundations established by the Strategic Plan for Judicial Innovations (SPJI) 2022-2027.
He also seeks to reinforce the court as both a place and a service, among other initiatives.
The justice said there should no longer be overburdened courts by 2032.
"While a courtroom or a courthouse is a physical representation of justice, the true measure of a court is not its buildings or facilities, but the quality of justice it provides," Marquez said.

"Citizens do not come to court because of the structure that houses it; they come because they seek protection of their rights, resolution of disputes, and assurance that the rule of law will prevail," he added.
The vacancy is due to the compulsorily retirement of Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo on November 6 at the age of 70. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Two men face UK national security charges following an incident near RAF Fairford, with police suspecting Iranian state involvement
articles.summary: British prosecutors have charged two men over an incident near RAF Fairford in September. Police suspect Iranian involvement in the case at a base used for US strikes on Iran.

image.caption: The base was used by US bombers to strike Iran and is at the center of an investigation into suspected Iranian-linked activity (FILE 28/09/2026)Image: Alastair Grant/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: British prosecutors said Tuesday that two men had been charged under the National Security Act in connection with a September incident near RAF Fairford, an airbase used by US forces to launch strikes on Iran.
US bombers were withdrawn from Fairford on security grounds shortly after arrests immediately after the incident.
What have police said about the Fairford suspects?

The Crown Prosecution Service charged Mohmed A., 24, of London, with engaging in conduct likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service. Counterterrorism police chief Laurence Taylor said investigators believed the country involved was Iran.
Nouman E., 24, also of London, was charged with entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK on August 22. Both men were due to appear in court later Tuesday.
Nouman E. was initially arrested near the Gloucestershire base on September 27 and rearrested on October 20.

A separate suspect, a 25-year-old British-Iranian dual national also arrested on October 20, was released without charge over the suspected intelligence offense. He remains on bail following an October 1 arrest on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts. Five other men also remain on police bail.
How did the Fairford investigation begin?

Armed police responded to reports of three suspicious vehicles near the base on September 27 and arrested five men. Scores of residents were evacuated as police and military bomb-disposal experts searched the area for explosives.
Police have said they consider Iranian state involvement "highly likely."
"We have seen a range of incidents in recent months that we believe have been directed by the Iranian state," Taylor said.
Iran has denied involvement, although it has previously said it considers bases used to attack its territory legitimate targets.

articles.title: Fears grow for Iranian athletes on death row as mountaineer latest to be hanged
articles.summary:
Two sportspeople have been executed in the past month and at least six more face the same fate, says activist group

Fears are growing for more Iranian athletes facing execution after…

blocks.text: Fears are growing for more Iranian athletes facing execution after mountain climber Ali-Sina Mostafavi became the latest in a string to be killed by the regime.

Mostafavi – who documented his ascents of some of the world’s highest peaks, including Mount Everest – was executed on 14 October having been arrested in April after the anti-government protests a few months earlier. His death followed the killing of Siavash Jamshidi Kheirabadi, a taekwondo athlete, at the start of October, and the mixed martial arts fighter Gholamreza Khani Shakarab, who was hanged in May.

Now Human Rights for Sport – a group of former Iranian athletes based in Oslo that has been documenting the growing number of cases – has warned that at least six more are facing execution after having their sentences upheld by Iran’s supreme court. They include the swimmer Ali Pishevarzadeh and the footballer Ehsan Hosseinpour, who were both arrested during the January protests, and Mohammad Javad Vafaei Sani – a boxer arrested in 2020 for taking part in protests a year earlier. He saw his request for a retrial rejected last year.

blocks.caption: Boxer Mohammad Javad Vafaei Sani – arrested for protesting in 2019 – is among those facing imminent execution, warns Human Rights for Sport. Photograph: Iran Human Rights

blocks.text: Another MMA fighter, Benyamin Naghdi, equestrian athlete Taraneh Rahimi and the climber Maryam Siri have also been condemned to death this year.
Human Rights for Sport said six athletes have already been executed in cases linked to the January protests or earlier political charges.

Dr Zohreh Abdollahkhani of Human Rights for Sport, said: “The Iranian sporting community is under enormous pressure.. For one of those sentenced to death, we managed to raise attention and awareness through other organisations and they halted his execution. But it was only temporary and I’m very concerned about all of them.”

Human Rights for Sport believe that athletes have been targeted to send a message to the wider community, with the deaths of prominent sportspeople often given widespread coverage in the state-run media. They include Navid Afkari Sangari – a wrestler who was executed in September 2020.

blocks.caption: Wrestler Navid Afkari Sangari was executed in September 2020. Photograph: UN Watch

blocks.text: “He was a role model and very famous in the whole community. What happened to him was also a warning to the whole population: look what we can do to someone like this,” Abdollahkhani said.

Mostafavi’s death sentence was upheld by the supreme court at the end of September and he is believed to have been subjected to physical violence during his detention in Kerman before being transferred to solitary confinement. He was accused of being an “armed agent of the American-Zionist enemy” and was arrested for allegedly opening fire on civilians in Azadi Square in Kerman on 24 March and taking part in January’s protests. Mostafavi’s family are thought to have been summoned to the prison hours before his execution.

blocks.caption: Mountaineer Ali-Sina Mostafavi before his detention. Photograph: Ali Sina Mostafavi/Facebook

blocks.text: Abdollahkhani said that making contact with those facing the death sentence is a challenge, as some members of their families are also being targeted by security services.
“In one case, his sister and brother-in-law have been arrested and the whole family’s phone lines are under surveillance. So it’s simply impossible to make direct contact,” she said.

Overall, Human Rights for Sport has found that 217 Iranian athletes were killed by direct gunfire in January, and more than 100 others detained. Four members of the European parliament also wrote to Fifa before the World Cup concerning Iranian athletes facing execution but Abdollahkhani said they received no response.

“Fifa is aware of the concerns raised regarding the situation of Iranian athletes and thanks all stakeholders for their continued collaboration and dedication to raising awareness of these critical matters,” a spokesperson for football’s governing body said.

Abdollahkhani also criticised the International Olympic Committee (IOC), saying changes in staffing had made it difficult to raise cases through its human rights and safeguarding structures. The IOC disputed her account, saying it had “fully functioning human rights and safeguarding teams”. It said it was deeply concerned about athletes affected by events in Iran but lacked the authority, as a non-governmental organisation, to change a sovereign country’s laws or political system.

“Within our remit, we work tirelessly with all stakeholders of the Olympic movement, including national Olympic committees and international federations, to support the creation of a safe sporting environment for all athletes. We will continue to work with our Olympic stakeholders to support all athletes globally through sports diplomacy, and we remain in touch with the Olympic community of Iran.”

articles.title: Bar examinees should excel in English, analytical skills --Dimaampao
articles.summary: Aside from knowledge of the law, Associate Justice Japar Dimaampao on Monday said he wants Bar examinees to possess a good command of the English language as well as analytical ability.

blocks.text: Published October 27, 2026 5:26pm
Aside from knowledge of the law, Associate Justice Japar Dimaampao on Monday said he wants Bar examinees to possess a good command of the English language as well as analytical ability.

During his interview with the Judicial and Bar Council (JBC), he was asked by Batangas Representative Gerville Luistro whether he is in favor of a more rigid law school to reduce the number of individuals who fail the exams.
“I am known as a strict but reasonable law professor. I only pass those who possess the three qualities,” he said.
“So I am in favor of a Bar examination that must test the analytical ability of the examinees. And if we are strict on that, there will be less passers,” he added.
When asked how the public may better understand decisions, Dimaampao said that a decision must be clear in reasoning, consistent in doctrine, concise, and just in result.

Meanwhile, Dimaampao proposed three initiatives to minimize graft and corruption. These are to strengthen independent accountability, institutionalize transparency and digitalization, and build a culture of integrity.
The vacancy is due to the compulsory retirement of Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo on November 6 at the age of 70.
Other candidates include Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen, Associate Justice Benjamin Caguioa, Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda, and Associate Justice Midas Marquez. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: NTC to monitor telco services, emergency radio groups during 'Undas'
articles.summary: The National Telecommunications Commission (NTC) on Tuesday said it will monitor telecommunications services and emergency radio groups during the Undas period from Oct. 31 to Nov. 2 as cemeteries…

blocks.text: Published October 27, 2026 5:24pm

The National Telecommunications Commission (NTC) on Tuesday said it will monitor telecommunications services and emergency radio groups during the Undas period from Oct. 31 to Nov. 2 as cemeteries and memorial parks prepare for increased public activity.

In a statement on Tuesday, the NTC said it had directed its regional offices to coordinate with telecommunications service providers to address reported service concerns, particularly in areas expected to experience increased mobile network traffic.

Regional directors were also instructed to coordinate with local government units, law enforcement agencies, disaster risk reduction and management offices, and emergency response units to support public safety operations.

The NTC said its regional offices would monitor Civic Action Groups (CAGs) and Amateur Radio Groups (ARGs) conducting public service activities, including the locations of their personnel, assistance posts, assigned routes and radio base stations.
These groups may serve as additional communication links for emergency response and public assistance during the holiday period, the agency said.

NTC Commissioner Ella Blanca Lopez underscored the importance of coordination among government agencies and the availability of reliable communications to help ensure public safety during the annual observance.
The agency advised the public to follow safety advisories, take note of local emergency hotline numbers, keep mobile phones charged and maintain contact with family members.)— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: What Marco Rubio’s sidestepping of New Delhi says about the US’s stance on India
articles.summary: Rubio’s decision not to meet Narendra Modi last week was seen by some as a snub – but by focusing on business leaders and oil, the secretary of state made American priorities clear. Plus: the…

blocks.text: When the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, visited India for the second time this year, headlines concentrated on who he met and where he went.

The fact that Rubio bypassed New Delhi and did not meet the prime minister, Narendra Modi, during his trip last week, and instead traveled to the financial capital, Mumbai, where he met India’s foreign minister, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar (pictured top with Rubio), and business leaders, did not go unnoticed. Nor did his decision to travel to Jamnagar, the small Gujarati town that is home to Reliance Industries’ colossal oil refinery complex.

Bilateral ties between the two countries have come under strain under the second Trump administration, particularly over tariffs and India’s purchase of Russian oil. Yet, Rubio’s return to India just five months after his first visit as secretary of state signals that the country remains useful for president Donald Trump’s ambitions after all.

As director of the South Asia Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, Milan Vaishnav has spent a decade tracking India’s place in the world, particularly its ties with the US. Vaishnav has described Trump 2.0 as “unbound” marking a new era in India-US relations.

Tracking foreign affairs, he told me, is a minefield right now. From the White House’s transactional approach to global alliances, ongoing conflicts in the Middle East and consequential elections around the world, politics is changing at a pace that means all predictions are off the table. “I think anyone who tells you they know exactly what is going on and how it fits into their neat theory of the world is lying to you,” says Vaishnav.
I asked him about the many confusing aspects of the US-India relationship, from the hostile political rhetoric to the US embrace of Pakistan, as well as Rubio’s latest visit.

blocks.caption: Marco Rubio speaking to the media in the Taj Mahal Palace hotel in Mumbai last Wednesday.  Photograph: Kylie Cooper/Reuters

blocks.text: Trump the deal-maker

Ahead of Rubio’s visit, several commentators noted the secretary of state’s “unusual” itinerary. Vaishnav thought the pre-visit chatter about Rubio skipping Delhi to visit Mumbai and Jamnagar was overblown. “Not every bilateral meeting has to take place in a national capital,” he says.

But that doesn’t mean it wasn’t noteworthy. “I do think the choice of venues was intentional. This administration and, particularly, this president, sees foreign policy through the lens of ‘deal-making’. And if you’re trying to drum up business deals, what better place to visit than Mumbai?” he says.

The Jamnagar visit, where Rubio met Mukesh Ambani, the chair of Reliance, also indicates some politicking. “At a time when petrol prices are extremely high in the United States and are likely to be a major issue in the 3 November midterm elections, the administration wants to show that it is doing everything it can to bring them down. India is a major consumer of oil, but it is also a major exporter of refined petroleum products,” says Vaishnav. “One of Rubio’s objectives was to encourage Reliance and, by extension, India to process more Venezuelan crude [oil],” he added.
While this could present an opportunity for India to advance relations, it’s not a given: the US president remains, after all – and to put it lightly – mercurial.

“The biggest plot twist for me has been the Trump administration’s embrace of Pakistan after the May 2025 conflict with India,” says Vaishnav. Pakistan’s standing in Washington had eroded over the years, especially under Joe Biden, who left office without ever having made a presidential phone call to his counterpart in Pakistan. “Many officials in Congress had grown exhausted with Pakistan’s double game, speaking the language of partnership on the one hand while undermining US interests on the other,” says Vaishnav.

But, after coming to power the second time, Trump thanked the country for its help in nabbing a suspect linked to a 2021 bombing in Afghanistan that killed 13 US service members. This reversal in Pakistan’s fortunes gathered pace after the May conflict with India, which Trump took credit for ending. In June, he welcomed Asim Munir, Pakistan’s army chief, to the White House, after Munir called for the president to be nominated for the Nobel peace prize.

“I chalk up the reversal to a few factors: Trump’s well-known strongman envy, Pakistan’s savvy diplomacy, and the prospect of energy and crypto deals involving members of Trump’s inner circle,” says Vaishnav. For him, it isyet another demonstration of how much weight Trump places on deals, transactions and short-term wins. “For New Delhi, this means Modi’s personal rapport with Trump and 25 years of investment in the bilateral relationship offer no guarantee against a 180-degree reversal in US policy,” he adds.

In a recent piece, Vaishnav’s colleague Sameer Lalwani pointed out that the US relationship with India remains more resilient than the political rhetoric may suggest with quiet, but nonetheless strategic, progress being made.

As Lalwani points out, bilateral trade reached a record high between India and the US in 2025; nearly $68bn worth of AI infrastructure investment in India has been pledged by US technology companies; and the two countries have carried out record number of joint military exercises this year.
The way forward

Despite these wins, in terms of future bilateral relations, “there are at least three reasons for caution,” warns Vaishnav. First, he points to the onslaught of US actions that have dented Indian interests. Trump had imposed a punitive 50% tariff on India in 2025, which was reduced to 18% earlier this year, but without a comprehensive trade deal being reached. Second, on immigration, the White House’s H-1B visa and green card restrictions have disproportionately affected Indian workers in Silicon Valley.

“This has created a real trust deficit on the Indian side, and with good reason,” says Vaishnav. The frustration was on display earlier this month, when New Delhi branded remarks made by the US vice-president, JD Vance, about Indian professionals as “deeply offensive”. Furthermore, Vaishnav argues that while governments and private sector firms might be great at making announcements, they’re not always a guarantee of delivery.

His final caution is how political tensions can have a chilling effect. The trade negotiations offer a telling example: in January, the US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, blamed the lack of a trade deal on Modi’s failure to phone Trump, a characterisation that New Delhi has disputed. Vaishnav says: “Much of the progress we are seeing is the product of decisions made years ago. It is one thing to keep existing projects moving, but turbulence in the relationship could make new initiatives a heavier lift.”

If India is serious about making its ambition to be a global powerhouse a reality, Vaishnav thinks there’s a clearcut way to win. “I would argue that the most important investment is political – ensuring India remains a robust, inclusive, participatory democracy,” he says. “On the economic front, India has made massive new investments in physical and digital infrastructure. But the returns on those investments will be limited unless the government doubles down on reforms: more efficient dispute resolution, an impartial legal system, even-handed tax enforcementand regulatory certainty.”
Ultimately, neither side can afford to treat the other as expendable. The test now is whether strategic foundations can hold at a time of global political upheaval.

blocks.text: Film-maker Ritu Sarin, director of the annual Dharamshala international film festival, which runs from 29 October to 1 November, suggests a film from this year’s lineup:

“Shot over three years on real locations, Anmol Sidhu’s sophomore feature, Flowers of Acacia, follows wedding orchestra dancers in rural Punjab with a gaze that allows all the large brutalities and smaller intimacies to shine through. Sidhu’s confident, consummate grasp of the medium is on full display in terrifying scenes that stretch to the edge of what is palatable. The camera refuses to look away.”
Count it
A number worth knowing

blocks.caption: Environmental activists have been protesting against the felling of trees, such as these marked for removal in a park in Versova, Mumbai.  Photograph: Alamy

blocks.text: That’s the number of trees Mumbai’s municipal authorities authorised to be felled over five months this year, to make way for development works, according to the Indian Express. Of these, about 3,500 will be permanently removed, while the rest will be replanted elsewhere.
Vibe check

blocks.caption: Prarthna Singh captured the rkivecity menswear line through a female gaze.   Photograph: Prarthna Singh

blocks.text: Prarthna Singh has consistently placed the female identity at the heart of her artistic practice, documenting Indian women’s aspirations and acts of rebellion in male-dominated spaces. When commissioned to photograph rkivecity’s menswear line, made from discarded clothes reworked into new garments, she turned that same gaze outward. The setting was the acclaimed 151-year-old Mayo College boys’ school in Ajmer, Rajasthan – Singh attended the linked girls’ school, and credits it with shaping her rebellious spirit.

“I was thinking about how I could bring a sense of intimacy and camaraderie of boarding-school life to the images, because that exists,” she told me. One image shows a pair of hands holding another boy’s jacket, the faces left out of the frame, so the garment stands in for the familiarity they share. Seeing this work against the backdrop of students taking to the streets to fight for their rights lends the series a lasting significance. “This was just my way of showing all of this is connected. These worlds are not existing separately,” said Singh.

articles.title: Two men charged with national security offences over RAF Fairford incident
articles.summary:
One charged assisting a foreign intelligence service and the other with entering a prohibited place, CPS says

Two men have been charged with national security offences after an investigation…

blocks.text: Two men have been charged with national security offences after an investigation into a suspected terror plot near RAF Fairford.
The Crown Prosecution Service said Mohmed Ahmad Abdulkarim, 24, and Nouman Essghir, 24, were both charged under the National Security Act 2023.

Abdulkarim, of London, has been charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service, while Essghir, also of London, has been charged with entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK.
They will appear at Westminster magistrates court on Tuesday.
Five other men arrested during the investigation remain on police bail.
Counter-terrorism police previously said it was “highly likely that there is Iranian state involvement” in the incident near the Gloucestershire base on 27 September.

Frank Ferguson, the chief crown prosecutor for the CPS special crime and counter-terrorism division, said: “The Crown Prosecution Service has decided to prosecute two individuals with National Security Act offences following a Counter Terrorism Policing investigation into a high-profile incident involving RAF Fairford.
“We will continue to work closely with our partners as this complex investigation continues.”
