articles.title: ABC to demand rightwing One Nation party stop using Bluey in ‘shocking and disrespectful’ cartoon
articles.summary:
Head of Australia’s national broadcaster says depiction of globally beloved character ramming politicians with a car breaches intellectual property

Australia’s national broadcaster will send…

blocks.text: Australia’s national broadcaster will send a cease and desist letter to rightwing populist party One Nation for using Bluey in a “shocking and disrespectful” cartoon which sees the beloved character repeatedly ramming politicians with an SUV.

ABC managing director Hugh Marks told Senate estimates on Tuesday he became aware of One Nation’s potential breach of intellectual property last week and sought legal advice. “We will be taking further action, I can assure you,” he said.

The legal dispute came to light after Western Australian Labor senator Varun Ghosh asked the ABC if it had sought legal advice over the 2024 political cartoon, called State of Melbourne, which has had 1.3m views on YouTube so far.
“I appreciate it was published two years ago, but has a particular poignancy in the last week,” Ghosh, the communications committee chair said.
Estimates was held a week after the alleged attack on independent MP Helen Haines outside the politician’s northern Victorian electorate office, which led to her losing both legs.
Marks said he believed the use is a clear breach of intellectual property and “a cease and desist letter should be issued”.

He revealed the ABC had been in contact with Bluey’s international distributor, BBC Studios, and the Brisbane-based creators Ludo. He said Pauline Hanson’s party had not sought permission to use the children’s character in the hit show. The BBC, Ludo and One Nation have been approached for comment.

“It’s not a parody of any Bluey work,” Marks said. “It’s not a minor use of the [intellectual property]. In my view, it is an infringement of the intellectual property, number one. But it’s also a shocking use of Australia’s most loved character.”
“In fact, probably the globally most loved character in a video. That is both shocking and disrespectful to the children of Australia who love that character so much.”

The animation shows Bluey behind the wheel striking a depiction of former Victorian premier Daniel Andrews and prime minister Anthony Albanese with an SUV, as well as TV host and conservationist Robert Irwin. Before he is run over the Albanese character says to Bluey: “You’ve got that crazy look in your eyes”.

In one scene in the three minute video Andrews is at the wheel, Albanese is his passenger and the car deliberately runs over Bluey and Irwin. The politicians are then shown putting the bodies of Bluey and Irwin in the boot of the SUV.
In other evidence at estimates, Marks said the ABC’s former news director, Justin Stevens, received a termination payout of $353,230 because he did not want him to work out his notice.
“Following Mr Stevens’s resignation, we had the option to ask Mr Stevens to continue to work through his notice period, or for me to ask him not to work out his notice period,” Marks said.
“I felt it was important, given what had happened, that I asked him not to work out his period, and to pay him his contractual entitlement to do so.
“I felt it was important that we move forward with new leadership. So I didn’t want to continue Mr Stevens in that role.”

Stevens, whose total remuneration for the financial year was $864,394, was replaced by Reuters executive Simon Robinson last month after a 19-year career at the public broadcaster. His base salary was $529,202, according to the annual report.
Marks told senators “mistakes” were made in the production of programs by former Four Corners reporter Mahmood Fazal but the entire leadership of Four Corners had now been replaced.
The ABC has removed several programs made by the sacked bikie-turned-journalist because of concerns over his use of anonymous interviewees.
“We did a review of Mr Fazal’s work and found substantial flaws in much of that work,” he said.
“I think we can take confidence that there are many great people who do work for Four Corners. And with new editorial leadership, we are obviously very confident as to its future.”
The ABC said it was reviewing its editorial guidance about the use of anonymous sources in light of the Fazal incident.
Sally Neighbour, a former Four Corners executive producer, alleged in the Monthly that “an associate of Fazal played different roles in different stories, disguised behind a mask”.

Fazal has previously said he stands by his reporting. In July, he said he was “shocked” by the removal of the two Four Corners episodes and that he believed the ABC’s process and decisions “set a worrying precedent for the organisation’s independence and commitment to public-interest journalism”.

articles.title: Tories dismiss PM’s budget ‘everyday fixes’ as little more than ‘cheaper gherkins’, and ‘an insult to families’ – UK politics live
articles.summary:
Removing tariffs on more than 100 products, including gherkins and baked beans, was one of five measures announced this morning before tomorrow’s budget

Good morning. Prime ministers tend to…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 3m agoUnison says focus on cost of living, including tax-free mileage, 'commendable', but 'bolder' policies needed
23m agoTories dismiss PM’s budget ‘everyday fixes’ as little more than ‘cheaper gherkins’, and ‘an insult to families

blocks.text: Unison says focus on cost of living, including tax-free mileage, 'commendable', but 'bolder' policies needed

Unison has particularly welcomed the announcement today about higher tax-free mileage rates being made permanent. (See 9.07am.) The union has been campaigning for this, and some of its members will benefit.
But, in her response, Andrea Egan, Unison’s general secretary illustrated how there is a limit to how much goodwill a government can generate from small “everyday fixes”. She said:

double quotation markThese are welcome measures, especially making the uplift to mileage rates permanent, something Unison has campaigned hard for. The government’s relentless focus on the cost of living is commendable. But the cost of essentials, including food and fuel, is going to keep soaring, meaning breathing space will quickly be closed down. That’s why we need to see a bolder approach, based on making the wealthy pay their fair share and improving the lives of working-class communities in a more enduring way.
The Treasury says three million people are expected to benefit from the mileage changes. It says:

double quotation markThese changes will provide £120 a year in additional tax savings for a worker doing 6,000 business miles, with someone driving 15,000 business miles receiving up to £300 in additional tax savings.
Tories dismiss PM’s budget ‘everyday fixes’ as little more than ‘cheaper gherkins’, and ‘an insult to families

Good morning. Prime ministers tend to get judged by posterity by the decisions they take on the big issues of the day. But little things matter too in the here and now, often disproportionately, and Andy Burnham, more than his predecessors, has decided that what he calls “everyday fixes” are worth focusing on too. Alexandra Topping wrote a good analysis about the pluses and minuses of this approach last week. But she filed too soon, because this morning Burnham has announced another five.

These are all changes contained in tomorrow’s budget but being announced today – presumably because John Healey will have bigger surprises for MPs tomorrow, and the Treasury wants these measures to get some media attention today because tomorrow they will be overshadowed by another story.

One of the measures is of particular interest to the Guardian because we have highlighted the scandal that led to hundreds of thousands of people getting the carer’s allowance being ordered to pay back huge sums of money because inadvertently their weekly earnings went slightly above the threshold allowed. In other parts of the welfare system, people just have to return the overpayment, but the rules for carer’s allowance were draconian, and a tiny breach of the weekly earnings allowance could lead to people being ordered to pay back thousands of pounds.
As Patrick Butler and Pippa Crerar report in our splash, this rule is being scrapped.
But this is one of just five “everyday fixes” announced this morning. Here is what the Treasury says about them.

double quotation mark• Making higher tax-free mileage rates permanent and increasing support for nurses, care workers, self employed builders and others who drive for work. The chancellor is locking in the 55p per mile rate for the first 10,000 business miles and increasing the rate above 10,000 miles from 25p to 35p per mile, supporting around 3 million employees and self-employed people who use their own vehicle for work. • Extending parental pay to more than 150,000 additional parents per year, including self-employed dads and partners who have previously missed out, giving eligible parents two weeks of support currently worth up to £194 a week so they can spend more time with their child. • Ending the Carer’s Allowance cliff edge, so unpaid carers no longer lose their entire allowance simply for earning a penny over the Weekly Earnings Limit, equivalent to 16 hours of the National Living Wage. Instead, only £1 of support will taper away for every additional £1 earned. • Removing import tariffs on more than 100 products, helping lower import costs on family favourites including baked beans, chocolate and gherkins, while also supporting farmers facing higher fertiliser bills and households that rely on kerosene heating oil. Together with tariff suspensions already introduced, households could save up to £21 on their food shop each year. • Rolling out hundreds more Post Office drop boxes, bringing the total to 1,000, making it easier and more convenient for people to send and return parcels without having to queue at a Post Office counter, helping take some of the hassle out of everyday errands in the run-up to Christmas. This comes alongside upgrades to 600 Post Office branches by the end of the financial year, improving services for customers across the country.
There is more detail in the Treasury news release here.
It is always easy to mock, and the Conservatives could not resist. Here is their response, from Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor.

double quotation markRampant borrowing, soaring taxes and an utter inability to cut spending mean inflation has already wiped out the benefits of Burnham’s ‘everyday fixes’. Shoppers face rising costs at the till and families are struggling to make ends meet, but Burnham’s plan is cheaper gherkins. This is an insult to families hammered by Labour’s tax rises.

The mention of gherkins in the Treasury press release did come as a surprise, given that they are not a key feature of the national diet, but maybe someone in Whitehall read the reports earlier this year about their importance for Pret a Manger sandwiches.
The problem with the Tory response is that, even though “everyday fixes” might not make a big difference, people tend to welcome them anyway. This is from Novara Media’s Aaron Bastani.

double quotation markPart of the genius with this stuff is the negative polarisation, when people start attacking perfectly sensible and helpful – albeit small – changes. Actually I want longer Post Office queues please!
Here is the agenda for the day.
10.30am: Sarah Sackman, the courts minister, gives evidence to the Lords justice committee on support for jurors.
Morning: Andy Burnham hosts a meeting with Muslim leaders in No 10.
11.30am: Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, takes questions in the Commons.
Noon: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.
After 12.30pm: Dan Jarvis, the security minister, is expected to give a statement to MPs about the government’s ‘Be Ready’ resilience advice about stockpiling essentials.

articles.title: N.S. woman refused to comply with phone scammer, so would-be fraudster swatted her house
articles.summary: A Truro-area woman says she is shaken and terrified after a would-be fraudster sent heavily armed police from two different departments to her home over the weekend.

image.caption: Lynn Clark Colpitts says a would-be fraudster sent heavily armed police officers from two different departments to her home over the weekend after she refused to go along with a scam. (Galen McRae/CBC)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia
A Truro-area woman says she is shaken and terrified after a would-be fraudster sent heavily armed police from two different departments to her home over the weekend.
'There's so many things that could have gone badly wrong,' says Lynn Clark Colpitts

The original call seemed like a routine phone scam. A woman claiming to be from the CIBC fraud department called Lynn Clark Colpitts and said someone had applied for a credit card in her name. In order to block it, she advised Clark Colpitts to download an app called CIBC Guard.

Colpitts said she didn’t feel comfortable doing that or sharing any information over the phone. While she was on the call she conferenced her IT expert from work into the call who told her to do nothing until she contacted her branch.
"I told her politely, I said I'm sorry I have to go by what my IT guy told me to do. And then she used some profanity toward me,” Clark Colpitts said.
“She called me a f-----g b---h, twice, and then hung up on me.”
Clark Colpitts figured she’d dodged a scam but 20 minutes later things escalated.
'She was threatening me the whole time'
“She calls me back and says, ‘I've got a surprise for you. Go to your front door. There's a surprise waiting for you there.’ And I'm like, ‘What are you talking about?’"
Sure enough, as she stepped onto her porch she saw heavily armed officers from the Colchester District RCMP and Truro Police in her yard and on the street.
“They holler at me and ask me who I am,” Clark Colpitts said. “And I tell them who I am and they tell me to get down to the end of the driveway.”

Several officers entered her home while Clark Colpitts tried to explain there was no such threat. While police checked on the property the fraudster kept up the phone calls to Clark Colpitts. She held it up so police could hear it.
“She was threatening me the whole time saying that she wasn't done with me and that this was gonna keep going on.”
RCMP explained to Clark Colpitts that they’d gotten a call about a hostage taking — and shooting — at her address.
Calls, emails and death threats
“It appears to be a level of retribution by the fraudsters in this case,” said Staff Sgt. Mark Rose, commander of the Colchester District RCMP.
“[It appears] they did this to cause her harm and pain and distress by having the police respond to her residence all because she didn’t follow the original instructions on the phone."
The calls from the female fraudster continued on Friday and into Saturday.
Staff Sgt. Mark Rose is the commander of the Colchester District RCMP. (Galen McRae/CBC)
“She just kept going on and on and on. It was relentless," Clark Colpitts said.
And there were emails too. Death threats.

Clark Colpitts is a realtor. She got a phone call from a coworker who said someone had hacked into their agency’s website, took down Clark Colpitts's photograph and replaced it with what Clark Colpitts says was a “deformed animal.” All of it has left her scared to be in her own home.
Swatting attack

David Shipley, CEO and co-founder of Beauceron Security, which is based in Fredericton, says Canadians have lost tens of millions of dollars to phone scams, but this is the first time he’s aware of it escalating into a “swatting” attack. That’s when a person calls police to someone’s property to report a crime or emergency that is entirely fiction.
“This seems like a criminal who was definitely not having a good day and decided to dramatically escalate the dangerousness and seriousness of this situation,” Shipley said.

“I would argue that this is a form of terrorism,” he said. “Canadians aren't used to having the SWAT team from the police department show up with assault rifles and body armour and riot shields to their front door. That's incredibly, incredibly traumatic.”

items: More stories from Northern Nova Scotia

blocks.text: Rose said police have to take these calls at face value and deliver the appropriate response.

“We've offered victim support services to [Clark Colpitts] and we are working with our law enforcement partners in other countries — and in Canada — to determine if this connects to other offences and try to determine who's responsible for this.”

CIBC told CBC News in a statement that there is no app called "CIBC Guard" and that it would never contact customers requesting personal or financial information, or request you download an app. It urged people to be extremely cautious when dealing with unsolicited emails, texts or phone calls, and not to rely on caller ID.
The bank said it's actively working to educate clients about impersonation and other scams, and it urges people to contact 911 if there is an urgent threat to their safety or the safety of others.
Meanwhile Clark Colpitts says she's traumatized.
“There's so many things that could have gone badly wrong.”

articles.title: Solidum says no need to hoard water as supply sufficient amid El Niño
articles.summary: There is no need to hoard water amid the El Niño phenomenon as supply remains sufficient in the next several months, Department of Science and Technology Secretary Renato Solidum Jr. said.

blocks.text: Published October 27, 2026 4:53pm

ANGELES, Pampanga —There is no need to hoard water amid the El Niño phenomenon as supply remains sufficient in the next several months, Department of Science and Technology Secretary Renato Solidum Jr. said.
"Dapat nga hindi nagho-hoard [ng tubig] because wala namang issue pa," Solidum said during a press conference in Angeles, Pampanga.
(People should not hoard water because there's no issue yet.)
He added that the public should not worry, especially in areas with well-managed dams and water conservation measures.
Solidum, instead, urged the public to save rainwater and use for household needs like washing the car and watering the plants.
"Bakit ka pa mag-i-imbak ng drinking water kung may supply pa naman? Kasi priority ng government niyan to supply the drinking water," Solidum said.
(Why store drinking water when there’s still a supply available? The government’s priority is to ensure the supply of drinking water.)
"But in case lang na may mga lugar na talagang walang-wala, then that's the time you actually use it (stored water)," he added.
(But only in cases where certain areas are completely without water should you actually use the water you’ve stored.)
As of 8 a.m., Angat Dam’s water level slightly decreased to 209.19 meters from 209.33 meters recorded on Sunday.
The dam's minimum operating level is 180 meters, while its normal high water level is at 210 meters.
Angat Dam supplies around 90% of the water needs of Metro Manila, Rizal, and portions of Cavite and Bulacan.

articles.summary: A woman from Mindanao on Tuesday filed an administrative complaint against her live-in partner, a police officer, over alleged abuse for nearly nine years, the National Police Commission (NAPOLCOM)…

blocks.text: Published October 27, 2026 4:52pm

A woman from Mindanao on Tuesday filed an administrative complaint against her live-in partner, a police officer, over alleged abuse for nearly nine years, the National Police Commission (NAPOLCOM) said.
In a statement, the NAPOLCOM said the complainant, who is a teacher, filed the complaint against Police Corporal Ricardo Silva Jr., who is assigned at Camp Crame in Quezon City.

“Hindi natin papayagan ang anumang uri ng karahasan laban sa kababaihan. Sa mga nakararanas ng pang-aabuso, huwag po kayong pumayag na saktan kayo, kahit sa unang pagkakataon pa lamang,” NAPOLCOM Commissioner Ralph Calinisan said at a press conference.
(We will not tolerate any form of violence against women. To those who are experiencing abuse, do not allow yourself to be harmed, even for the first time.)
“Magsumbong po kayo sa awtoridad. Nandiyan ang PNP at ang NAPOLCOM para makinig, tumulong, at umalalay sa inyo,” he added.
(Report it to the authorities. The PNP and NAPOLCOM are here to listen, help, and support you.)
Calinisan vowed to pursue appropriate administrative proceedings against Silva for grave misconduct and conduct unbecoming of a police officer.
During the press briefing, the complainant, identified as alias “Ma’am” recounted how she sought help after feeling that she could no longer escape her abusive situation.

“Sa lahat ng battered women diyan, oras na po para lumabas kayo. Huwag n’yo na pong tiisin. Huwag niyo nang hintayin na masiraan kayo ng bait, mawala ang mga pangarap n’yo sa buhay, o mawala ang mga pinaghirapan ninyo. Huwag n’yo nang hintaying sirain kayo ng isang taong hindi naman karapat-dapat,” she said.

(To all the battered women out there, it's time to come out. Don't put up with it anymore. Don't wait for your sanity, dreams, or things you worked hard for to be destroyed. Don't wait for someone who doesn't deserve it to destroy you.)
For his part, Silva apologized for his actions and urged fellow police officers not to follow his example.

“Sorry, Hon, sa nagawa ko. Sa mga kabaro ko, huwag n’yo akong tularan. Kung masama man ang loob n’yo, magdasal na lang. Sa lahat ng tao, humihingi po ako ng paumanhin sa mali kong nagawa,” Silva said during the press conference.
(Sorry, Hon, for what I did. To my colleagues, don't imitate me. If you have bad feelings, just pray. To everyone, I apologize for the wrong I did.) —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: China's Liaoning aircraft carrier group in PH waters 'no cause for alarm' --AFP
articles.summary: The passage of China's Liaoning aircraft carrier group through Philippine waters is “no cause for alarm,” the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) said Tuesday.

blocks.text: Published October 27, 2026 4:29pm
The passage of China's Liaoning aircraft carrier group through Philippine waters is “no cause for alarm,” the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) said Tuesday.

At a press briefing, AFP spokesperson for the West Philippine Sea Rear Admiral Roy Vincent Trinidad said the movement was part of the Chinese People's Liberation Army Navy's (PLAN) periodic exercises.
“It is no cause for alarm. It is not the first time that a carrier battle group of the PLAN has transited international and Philippine waters,” Trinidad said.
“What happened recently is part of an annual, twice a year, periodic aircraft carrier operation exercise, training exercise, conducted by the PLA Navy,” he added.
The Liaoning last week followed a route along the country's western seaboard, coming within 15 nautical miles of the Philippine landmass before exiting southward, according to the AFP official.

He said the carrier group's usual route involves passing through the Bashi or Balintang Channel, proceeding along the eastern seaboard toward Australia, and returning through the Sibutu Passage and the West Philippine Sea.
“Every month we monitor approximately 16,000 different maritime merchant and naval assets passing through our waters,” he said.

“Of these approximately 16,000 all of them are challenged. Around 3,000 do not respond. The aircraft carrier Liaoning did not respond to our challenge. They are not the only ones who do not respond,” he added.

Asked whether the carrier group's passage constituted an incursion into Philippine waters, Trinidad cited the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), saying foreign vessels are allowed innocent passage through a coastal state's archipelagic waters.
A typical carrier strike group includes destroyers, air-defense destroyers, other surface vessels, replenishment ships, and is expected to have a submarine, according to Trinidad.

He said the AFP's Western Mindanao Command reported that the Liaoning exited southward. However, he could not immediately provide the exact date, time, and location of the carrier group's exit. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Who replaces VP Sara? Lacson says Cayetano can’t tie Marcos’ hands
articles.summary: Sen. Ping Lacson questioned why Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano would ask senator-judges to swear off the vice presidency, saying the choice of Vice President Sara Duterte’s…

blocks.text: October 27, 2026 | 4:06pm
In this undated photo shows Sen. Alan Peter Cayetano and Sen. Ping Lacson.
Senate SMU

MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Ping Lacson questioned why Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano would ask senator-judges to swear off the vice presidency, saying the choice of Vice President Sara Duterte’s successor, should she be convicted, belongs to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. alone.
Lacson said Cayetano’s appeal was “uncalled for” when he spoke to reporters on the sidelines of a Senate budget hearing on Monday.
Cayetano had urged his fellow senator-judges to follow Sen. Chiz Escudero, who said he would refuse the vice presidency if Duterte is convicted, citing a conflict of interest.
"Bakit niyang pakikialaman ang prerogative ng pangulong pumili? Bakit siya lilimitahan? I think it's uncalled for na pangunahan niya ang pangulo," Lacson told reporters on Monday, October 26.
(Why would he interfere with the president’s prerogative to choose? Why would he limit it?)

In a later statement on social media, Lacson wrote that "someone had the gall to suggest that my Senate colleagues should decline a VP appointment" if the trial results in conviction and Duterte needed to be replaced.
The question of who, if ever, would be appointed to the position of vice president is already cropping as the Duterte impeachment trial enters its last stretch.

Under the 1987 Constitution, the president fills a vacancy in the vice presidency by nominating a member of the Senate or the House of Representatives, and a majority of each chamber, voting separately, must confirm the choice.
A conviction would remove Duterte from office and could bar her from running for president in 2028.
As a hypothetical, Lacson said if the president decided to appoint Sen. Lito Lapid, it would be a "foolish proposition" for the senator to turn the request down.
He asked whether Lapid should have to decline “simply because he is a senator-judge,” then added: “Isn’t that a foolish proposition?”
Lacson said he has no interest in the post himself. His Senate term runs until 2031, and he said he would decline the vice presidency if it were offered.

“All of us senator-judges should make this declaration,” he said on Monday. He argued that senator-judges should have no “incentive” to convict Duterte and should base their verdict only on the evidence. In a later Facebook post, Cayetano wrote that Escudero “could have kept quiet and left the possibility open,” and had instead given the public a reason to trust his vote. “Everyone remains free to decide,” Cayetano added.
Cayetano said in a social media post Tuesday that senators "should not discuss a successor as though a conviction were already certain."
"But when should we make clear that we will put personal interests aside? Must we wait until we have voted or someone offers us the position?" he said.

Lacson and Cayetano have feuded through much of the trial and traded accusations of wrongdoing: Lacson has hounded Cayetano with accusations of corruption and attempting to block probes into flood control works in Taguig City.
Cayetano, meanwhile, has accused Lacson of having a questionable increase in his declared net worth and of acting as a "one-man justice department."

articles.title: US War chief Hegseth to visit PH; China invited to ASEAN defense meeting --DND
articles.summary: United States Secretary of War Pete Hegseth is expected to visit the Philippines on Wednesday for the ASEAN Defense Ministers' Meeting (ADMM) - Plus, the Department of National Defense (DND) said…

blocks.text: Published October 27, 2026 4:05pm

United States Secretary of War Pete Hegseth is expected to visit the Philippines on Wednesday for the ASEAN Defense Ministers' Meeting-Plus (ADMM), the Department of National Defense (DND) said Tuesday.
At a press conference, DND spokesperson Assistant Secretary Arsenio Andolong said the Philippines was expecting Hegseth's visit.
However, Andolong said he could not yet provide details on the specific outcomes of Hegseth’s engagements with Philippine officials.

“At this point in time, I am unable to provide any information. However, I must say that on Thursday, during the turnover address of [Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr.], he will provide information on this,” he said.
Manila’s broad priorities in its bilateral relations with the US include strengthening the alliance, defense modernization, and future capacity- and capability-building, according to Andolong.
The Philippines is set to host the 20th ADMM and the 13th ADMM-Plus from October 28 to 29 in Lapu-Lapu City, Cebu, with the theme "Navigating Our Future Together."
Meanwhile, China has been invited to participate in the meetings, but its attendance has yet to be confirmed.
“What I know is that an invitation was extended, but as of this moment, we have no confirmation of their attendees,” Andolong said.
The ADMM is ASEAN's highest defense consultative and cooperative mechanism.
The ADMM-Plus, established in 2010, expands defense cooperation to eight dialogue partners including Australia, China, India, Japan, New Zealand, South Korea, Russia, and the United States.

Andolong said the South China Sea and the West Philippine Sea are expected to be among the topics discussed during the meetings. He noted that these maritime issues are almost always part of the ADMM discussions.

Other anticipated areas of cooperation include maritime security, humanitarian assistance and disaster response, counterterrorism, peacekeeping operations, military medicine, humanitarian mine action, and cybersecurity.
The Philippines will formally turn over the ADMM and ADMM-Plus chairship to Singapore on Thursday.

The meetings also coincide with the 50th anniversary of the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation in Southeast Asia, which upholds respect for sovereignty, non-interference, and the peaceful settlement of disputes. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Gatchalian calls for penalties vs power firms over outages, high rates
articles.summary: Gatchalian is pressing regulators over outages and high electricity prices.

blocks.text: October 27, 2026 | 4:05pm
An electric lineman repairs a power line along Jupiter Street in Makati on March 25, 2026, amid rising electricity costs and concerns over the country's energy supply.
The STAR / Ryan Baldemor

MANILA, Philippines — Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian called on the Department of Energy (DOE) and the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) on Tuesday, October 27, to hold erring power firms accountable amid high electricity prices and recurring grid alerts in the Visayas and Mindanao.

"Other than brownout alerts, electricity rates in the Visayas and Mindanao are also extremely high. We cannot let this go unaddressed. The DOE needs to come up with concrete solutions," Gatchalian said in Filipino.
He said generation companies that fail to perform or engage in abusive practices should face heavy penalties, while the DOE and ERC should work together to address the problem.
In a separate interview, ERC Legal Service Director Maria Corazon Gines said a secondary price cap is in place in the Wholesale Electricity Spot Market (WESM) to limit sustained price spikes.

Under the current rules, the P7,423-per-megawatt-hour secondary price cap takes effect when the 72-hour rolling average electricity price exceeds P12,413 per MWh. The mechanism is triggered automatically once the threshold is breached and does not require a separate ERC announcement.
Gines said the commission is coordinating with the DOE to prepare the power sector for higher demand during El Niño.
"The DOE and ERC are urging plants to complete their preventative maintenance activities so that when El Niño arrives, these plants are immediately ready to supply power," Gines said.
Visayas grid under alert
The statements come as the Visayas grid continues to experience tight power supply and recurring red and yellow alerts.
The grid was again placed under red and yellow alerts Tuesday, with the red alert scheduled from 5 p.m. to 7 p.m. and yellow alerts from 3 p.m. to 5 p.m. and again from 7 p.m. to 9 p.m.
Power plant outages and reduced generation capacity have repeatedly cut available supply to the grid in recent weeks.
According to grid data cited Tuesday, 24 plants were on forced outage, while another 19 were operating at reduced capacity, leaving 811.6 megawatts unavailable to the grid.

articles.title: Why a spate of gun-for-hire shootings in Toronto were likely paid for by Iran

image.caption: Police take photos of a bullet hole at the scene of an early morning shooting outside the U.S. Consulate in Toronto, on July 27. The attack was among a dozen politically-motivated gun-for-hire incidents that may have been sponsored by the Iranian government. (Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Investigates·New
A CBC News investigation has pinpointed a dozen politically-motivated gun-for-hire shootings in Toronto that appear to have been financed by the Iranian government.
Attacks on Jewish, U.S. and anti-regime targets fit worldwide pattern of violence
· CBC News
· Posted: Oct 27, 2026 4:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 31 minutes ago
The attacks targeted synagogues, a school and businesses in the Greater Toronto Area, as well as the U.S. Consulate in the city's downtown.
With many of the shootings coming in the hours and days after the United States and Israel began bombing Iran on Feb. 28 and assassinated the country's Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

No one was injured in the Toronto shootings, all of which bore the hallmarks of gun-for-hire incidents: early morning attacks where suspects arrived via stolen cars and emptied handguns into building entranceways, while they — or their accomplices — filmed the acts on a phone.
There’s a gig economy for gunmen in Toronto. Is Iran hiring them?

Toronto Police, the RCMP and CSIS have been investigating whether a foreign power instigated the politically-motivated attacks. But while some of the alleged trigger men have been arrested and charged, it has been harder to determine just who was paying them.
The gun-for-hire model, where shootings are arranged via encrypted apps and intermediaries, provides several layers of separation between the client and the criminal.

"We have heard information that there may be foreign actors that are involved. We are investigating every angle," said Chief Superintendent Joe Matthews, who is overseeing the Toronto Police Service investigation.

"At this point, I'm not willing to confirm or deny that piece of it, but what I will say is that we don't think there's a very direct connection between the financier and the perpetrator on the street."

CBC News spent weeks researching a slew of shootings in Toronto, obtaining court files where arrests have been made, and building profiles of the accused. Most of the suspects face charges for multiple attacks. Many are young — ranging in age from 15 to their early 20s.

items: Organized crime is using encrypted messaging apps to enlist youth. This spells trouble for police
2 people, including 15-year-old, facing multiple charges after gunshot fired at U.S. consulate in Toronto
Teen sentenced for 1st-degree murder in death of tow truck driver at Scarborough gas station

blocks.text: What emerged was a pattern — shootings concentrated in the same corners of the city, over the same night — directed at both political and non-political targets. In several incidents, synagogues and Jewish-owned businesses were hit shortly before, or after, attacks on nearby business and residential addresses associated with waste management giant, Green For Life (GFL).
Toronto Police say ballistic tests confirm that link.
“We're seeing firearms that are being used in multiple shootings that aren't just geopolitical targeted, they are crossing over with GFL,” Matthews told CBC News.
All of which points to the same people — hired guns — having carried out both types of attacks.
In recent years, the Iranian government and its intelligence service have been linked to plots and attacks in Germany, the Netherlands, the U.K., Australia and the United States.

Last May, the FBI arrested Mohammad Baqer al-Saadi, whom they claim is a senior member of Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI), a militia group controlled by Iran's Revolutionary Guard. He now faces six terrorism related charges.

The indictment filed in New York State, alleges he helped plan and co-ordinate at least 18 attacks in Europe, as well as two more in Canada — the March 2026 shooting at the U.S. Consulate in Toronto and an assault on an unnamed synagogue.
Police cordoned off the street in front of the U.S. Consulate in Toronto on July 27. They said a firearm was discharged at the building in the early morning hours. (Paul Smith/CBC)
In June, Canada issued a joint statement with 20 other nations, condemning Iran's "lethal plotting and other malign actions" in Europe, North America and Australia.
"The relationship between Iranian security services and international and local criminal groups is long standing," the statement read. "Their use of these groups is deplorable."
Still, allegations of Iranian subterfuge continue, most recently in the U.K., following a foiled plot to attack a Royal Air Force base in England.

items: U.K. counter-terror police arrest British-Iranian suspect over Fairford air base investigation
Australia accuses Iran of being behind two antisemitic attacks, orders ambassador to leave

blocks.text: The Iranian-linked attacks follow the same blueprint that Russia has been using to sow havoc in Europe since its invasion of Ukraine, said Keir Giles, a security analyst at Chatham House, an independent policy institute in London.

"Certainly the Russian use of this kind of approach, they pushed the boundaries further and faster," said Giles. "But inevitably, once a technique or a method of achieving these nefarious aims has been demonstrated, other people will latch on."
Gun-for-hire attacks, or Violence as a Service (VAAS) as it is also known, have been supercharged by the internet and the spread of encrypted communication apps, Giles said.

"It's always been the case that you could recruit willing, or unwilling, or even unknowing dupes to carry out your attacks for you," he said. "But it's become vastly easier to spread your network, to actually reach and recruit them at really, very little cost."

CBC News reached out to Iran’s Foreign Ministry to ask about Tehran's alleged involvement in the Toronto attacks, but did not receive a response. The Iranian government has dismissed past claims that it has sponsored violence around the world.
Beth Avraham Yoseph of Toronto (BAYT), was one of the synagogues that was attacked in early March 2026. Its front doors and windows peppered with gunfire late on a Friday night.
A bullet hole in a glass door at Beth Avraham Yoseph of Toronto (BAYT) synagogue following a March 2026 gun-for-hire attack. (Submitted by BAYT)
Rabbi Daniel Korobkin says there was anger and frustration following the shooting, but that the congregation refuses to be intimidated.

"We recognize that there are many players that are making Israel and Jews as the pariah of the story. We're used to it," Korobkin said. "It's not going to deter us from being Jews. It's not going to deter us from coming to synagogue."
Korobkin is aware that the attack on his synagogue may have been ordered and paid for by someone living thousands of miles away. But to him, it hardly matters.

"I don't think it really makes a difference whether the person who hates us is pulling the trigger, or paying a person to pull the trigger," he said. "The end result is the same and we just want it to stop and we need to figure out how we can control it in the future."

Jonathon Gatehouse has covered news and politics at home and abroad, reporting from dozens of countries. He has also written extensively about sports, covering seven Olympic Games and authoring a best-selling book on the business of pro-hockey. He works for CBC's national investigative unit in Toronto.

articles.title: Canadian 'tremendously sorry' after spending stolen crypto on Lamborghini, BMWs, jewelry
articles.summary: A 20-year-old Canadian who conned cryptocurrency holders out of millions of dollars — and lived large as a teenager in Florida with "extravagant" partying, access to a private jet and luxury cars —…

image.caption: Canadian Trenton Johnston was 19 at the time of his arrest in March 2026 in North Miami. He was sentenced Monday to time served after pleading guilty to a money laundering conspiracy and handing over $3.8 million US worth of stolen cryptocurrency. (Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office)

blocks.text: World·New

A 20-year-old Canadian who conned cryptocurrency holders out of millions of dollars — and lived large as a teenager in Florida with "extravagant" partying, access to a private jet and luxury cars — could soon be headed home to Canada after he pleaded guilty to a money laundering conspiracy and was sentenced to time served Monday.
Trenton Johnston sentenced to time served after pleading guilty to U.S. money laundering conspiracy

A 20-year-old who conned cryptocurrency holders out of millions of dollars — and lived large as a teenager in Florida with "extravagant" partying and access to a private jet and luxury cars — could soon be headed home to Canada.

A U.S. federal judge in Miami on Monday sentenced Trenton Richard David (Trent) Johnston to time served after he pleaded guilty to a money laundering conspiracy and handed over $3.8 million US worth of stolen crypto.

Johnston, then 19, was seated in the back of a Rolls-Royce Cullinan SUV that smelled of "freshly burned marijuana" when he was arrested in March, according to court documents. He's been in custody ever since.

U.S. Homeland Security Investigations found Johnston, a Canadian citizen, impersonated Google tech support staff and representatives of crypto firms to convince unwitting victims to share the codes to their cryptocurrency wallets.
The scheme made him a fortune.
Johnston was arrested after he was found with suspected amphetamine tablets in a Hermes bag while seated in the back of this Rolls-Royce Cullinan. (EpicVIN)
Prosecutors detailed 'extravagant' lifestyle

In one instance in March, Johnston and an unnamed co-conspirator swindled a victim in California out of his life savings — 185 bitcoin, or the equivalent of about $13 million US at the time, court documents say.

"We actually smacked a 185btc target today," Johnston wrote in a series of text messages to his accomplice, according to a criminal complaint filed in U.S. District Court in Miami. "Club feels mad good after today."
"And we ain't done," he added.
Prosecutors said Johston splurged on "an extravagant nightlife and entertainment lifestyle" while living in the Miami area, where he relocated in 2024.
Some of his big-ticket purchases are laid out in court documents: a high-powered Lamborghini Aventador SVJ, two BMWs, jewelry and a private jet rental.
He didn't hide the ruse. According to a witness interviewed by investigators, Johnston showed others how he carried out the thefts by sharing his screen over the social platform Discord.

items: 'Crypto King' trial hears recording of Aiden Pleterski admitting $300M fund 'never existed'

blocks.text: Johnston's defence lawyer Brooke C. Watson said in a recent court filing that after his arrest, the Canadian "turned over all of the stolen cryptocurrency in his possession," approximately $3.8 million US in bitcoin and ether, another typo of cryptocurrency.
"Mr. Johnston quickly admitted his conduct and is tremendously sorry for what he has done," Watson wrote.

Johnston had overstayed his 12-month U.S. tourist visa after crossing from Fort Erie, Ont., to Buffalo, N.Y., in October 2024 at age 18. But the lawyer revealed in a court filing last week that Johnston's scheme started months earlier — when he was just 17 — in January 2024.

In a court filing before sentencing, a defence lawyer for Johnston included pictures titled 'Trenton Johnston, growing up in Canada.' The name of his hometown is redacted in the court documents. (U.S. District Court, Southern District of Florida)
Hometown redacted in court documents

Watson did not respond to CBC News when asked where in Canada Johnston is from. His hometown and the names of his parents — a mechanic and a hair stylist — are redacted in court documents filed last week ahead of sentencing.

In a plea deal, federal prosecutors agreed to withdraw a wire fraud conspiracy charge in exchange for Johnston's guilty plea to one count of conspiracy to commit money laundering. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida had previously announced that Johnston faced 20 years in prison if convicted on both counts.
Prosecutors later said Johnston provided "substantial assistance in the investigation and prosecution" of other unnamed individuals.

items: Canadian cybersecurity exec arrested by FBI accused of working with criminals to defraud his own clients

blocks.text: He still faces a drug possession charge from Florida state prosecutors stemming from amphetamine pills found in a Hermes bag at the time of his March arrest in the back of that Rolls-Royce Cullinan in North Miami.
It's unclear when Johnston will be released from custody.
He already agreed to a removal order issued in April by a U.S. immigration judge.
Eventually, Johnston is expected to be handed over to the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to be deported to Canada.
If you have a news tip related to this story, contact CBC News senior reporter Thomas Daigle by email: thomas.daigle@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Long-term medication or modern crash diet? Inside the new world of GLP-1s
articles.summary: GLP-1s were designed and tested for long-term use, to combat chronic health conditions like diabetes and obesity. But what happens when you take these blockbuster weight loss drugs for a short stint?…

image.caption: GLP-1s were designed and tested for long-term use to combat chronic health conditions like diabetes and obesity. But what happens when you take these blockbuster weight loss drugs for a short stint? Scientists are trying to find out. (Matthew Hoddy/CBC)

blocks.text: At a bridal shop in downtown Halifax, Beverley Smith is trying on wedding dresses, but there’s a catch: She's rapidly losing weight since starting a GLP-1.

The 32-year-old has already gone on and off several types of these popular medications to manage weight gain and other side-effects linked to polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), but decided to get serious about her health before getting married next summer.
She’s lost more than 30 pounds since starting the drug tirzepatide back in March, and says related symptoms — like joint pain — have improved as well.
Now she’s asking the same question as millions of GLP-1 users around the world: Is it possible to one day stop taking the drug that’s changed life for the better?
"When you are going off it…. do you taper off of it or do you stop abruptly?" Smith wondered. "What is this really going to look like in the long term?"
As these blockbuster drugs explode in popularity, with more people using them off-label for short-term weight loss, scientists are also striving to find an answer.
"This is a real-world situation that needs to be studied," said Dr. Thomas Leung, a clinician-scientist at the University of Pennsylvania, who’s among the researchers doing exactly that.
Microdosing, drug cycling and more
GLP-1 drugs work by suppressing blood sugar, controlling appetite and slowing stomach emptying, all by mimicking their namesake hormone, glucagon-like peptide-1, which is released after you eat.

items: 3 million Canadians use GLP-1 drugs. Survey says that's changing their appetites — and habits
Should everyone be on GLP-1s? What the science really tells us about cancer prevention and other benefits

blocks.text: While these medications only became part of the zeitgeist in the last few years — driven by celebrity endorsements, before hitting the mainstream — they’ve been around for more than two decades.

The earliest forms were studied and approved to treat Type 2 diabetes. Later, options arrived for chronic weight management. What’s relatively new is the myriad ways people are using these medications, often with minimal medical supervision.

At a private appointment inside Kind Bridal in Halifax, Beverley Smith tries on a wedding dress and discusses alterations to accommodate her ongoing weight loss while using a GLP-1. (Hugo Levesque/CBC)
Many patients — or as some drugmakers now call them, "customers" — are treating GLP-1s like a yo-yo diet rather than taking them long term to manage chronic health conditions.

They’re ever easier to get through online pharmacies. And pill forms, versus injections, are becoming more accessible. (Though not yet available in Canada, there is a pill-based form of semaglutide — the drug best known by the brand name Ozempic — already approved in the U.S. from drugmaker Novo Nordisk, alongside a pill version of orforglipron from Eli Lilly.)

items: 1st generic semaglutide injection for weight loss approved: Health Canada

blocks.text: Scroll through social media and it’s easy to find a range of short-term uses, from bodybuilders cycling through different types of GLP-1s (and steroids, too) alongside their gym routines to women "microdosing" the drugs off and on to manage menopausal weight gain to brides and grooms doing quick stints to lose weight before their wedding day.
One recent study from a Danish research team looked at the use of semaglutide for obesity and found roughly half of adults stopped treatment within just 12 months.
Ozempic, other GLP-1 drugs may help with dozens of other conditions
Stop-and-start approach could hinder weight loss

It’s a trend Dr. Leung, the researcher from the University of Pennsylvania, noticed in his own social circle in recent years, as more of his friends and colleagues wanted to try GLP-1s just to drop a few pounds.

Some talked about wanting to shed weight before a vacation or to look good on Instagram or just to feel healthier. The common thread? A desire to go on the meds, then get off them as fast as possible.

"No one had really studied what happens when you model what human behaviour is, which is starting and stopping these drugs," Leung said. "So we’re like, OK, well, obviously you can’t test this in humans. But we can try to do this in mice."

items: Generic Ozempic is now about $100 a month across the country. Canadians are taking note
Health Canada approves 1st generic version of Novo Nordisk's Ozempic

blocks.text: Leung and his research team did exactly that, and found cycling overweight mice through GLP-1 use seemed to make the drugs less effective over time. Mice who started and stopped the drugs every two weeks struggled to lose weight compared to mice who stayed on GLP-1s for the entire months-long study.
Even after two months of consistent use at the end of the study period, the drug-cycling group remained 20 per cent heavier.
If that was happening to mice, Leung started to wonder: What’s actually happening inside the bodies of human patients stopping and starting these body-changing drugs?
Ozempic: the future of addiction treatment?
'Buyer beware' when using GLP-1s off-label
Dr. Sean Wharton sees that regularly in his own patients at the Wharton Medical Clinic for weight and diabetes management in Burlington, Ont.
"People are using it off-label often. Maybe they heard about something on the internet or on Facebook. And if they're using it in this manner off-label, then it’s … buyer beware," he said.
"Because I don't know what type of negative aspects could potentially happen. There could be mainly positive and no negative aspects, but we don't exactly know yet."

items: People regained weight, worsened heart health after stopping weight loss drugs: review
Health Canada warns about fake or unauthorized versions of GLP-1 drugs

blocks.text: Wharton stressed this growing class of drugs has clear benefits as a long-term treatment for obesity, which has a dangerous domino effect on other health issues, like inflammation and cardiovascular disease, when left untreated.
Research also suggests GLP-1s may help curb substance use disorders, cut the severity of sleep apnea or even reduce cancer risk.
Dr. Sean Wharton is an internal medicine specialist and clinical researcher in obesity medicine in Toronto. (Craig Chivers/CBC)

Yet increasingly, these drugs are moving from tested treatment into what Wharton calls the "aesthetic medicine space" for short-term use. And he says the benefits likely vanish when patients rush back off these drugs.

"If losing the weight was the reason why your metabolic condition — like your heart failure, your high blood pressure — got better, then regaining the weight usually means that that blood pressure is going to go back up."

items: Ozempic use, protein-maxxing driving up whey protein prices
We know junk food isn't healthy, but scientists are trying to determine if it's also bad for our brains

blocks.text: Last year, one major research review concluded that the "magnitude and consistency" of these kinds of health effects "underscore the physiological consequences of [GLP-1] discontinuation."
A key need, according to that research team, was treatment guidelines to also address how to stop using the drugs.
What's the best way to go off these drugs?

GLP-1 pioneer Dr. Daniel Drucker agrees with that approach. In Toronto, he’s helping lead a randomized controlled trial — the gold standard of health-care research — to find out the best way for people to safely stop taking the drugs that he helped bring to the masses.

The research team, which includes Wharton and Drucker’s colleague and fellow endocrinologist Dr. Caroline Kramer, is recruiting patients for a 16-week-long study period where they’ll go through regular bloodwork and other metrics to gauge the impact of slowly tapering off a GLP-1 compared to abruptly stopping.

items: How do semaglutides or GLP1's work?

blocks.text: "We’re trying to answer a very simple question: If someone wants to know, can they come off the GLP-1 medicines, what is the best way to do it?" Drucker told CBC News inside a lab at Mount Sinai Hospital.
"Pharmaceutical companies are not good at studying how to stop their medicine," Drucker said, "but we need to answer that question."

GLP-1 researchers Dr. Caroline Kramer, left, and Dr. Daniel Drucker are studying the best way to stop using these blockbuster drugs through a trial based out of Mount Sinai Hospital in Toronto. (Lauren Pelley/CBC)

Drucker is among those who sees huge potential for GLP-1s as a way to reduce the dire impacts of obesity — a public health crisis so widespread that just this year, the World Health Organization released its first-ever guidelines to manage obesity starting from childhood.

But tackling long-term medical issues usually requires long-term treatment, he stressed. When you discontinue minoxidil for hair regrowth, for example, hair loss restarts. If you suddenly stop taking statins, cholesterol spikes fast. Why would GLP-1s be any different?

"There is a lot of stigma around staying on a medicine to control your body weight for long periods of time, but we would never have anyone question if they had MS or Crohn's or hypertension or high cholesterol," Drucker said.

"I could list at least 125 diseases where you take the medication for the rest of your life to control the disease, but for some reason with the GLP-1 medicine, people think, well, you should be able to do this yourself."
Short-term use may 'cause more harm than good'
Kramer said there really hasn’t been research to help show if the cardiovascular benefits of being on a GLP-1 can be maintained by gradually tapering off rather than quickly stopping.
The team will also be watching for symptoms and adverse events, given there can be a range of side-effects from common stomach upset to acute pancreatitis to rare reports of vision loss.

items: What does thin mean in the age of GLP1s?
Why cheaper weight loss drugs could be a 'gamechanger' for Canadians

blocks.text: Kramer's advice for Canadians who want to do a short-term stint on a weight-loss drug before her team’s results come in?
"Patients who want to shed, like, three pounds because, ‘I have a wedding in two weeks’ … that is not what the medications were meant for," she said.
"If you are thinking of taking a medication without the proper assessment over a short term … it may cause more harm than good."

articles.title: As scandals mount, data shows drop in street-level experience among Montreal police
articles.summary: Newly obtained internal data reveals a drop in experience levels at Station 39, where a group of officers were suspended this summer for alleged hateful and discriminatory acts. Experts and former…

image.caption: Montreal police officers walk into Station 39 in Montreal, on Saturday, June 13, 2026. (Graham Hughes/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Montreal

Newly obtained internal data reveals a drop in experience levels at Station 39, where a group of officers were suspended this summer for alleged hateful and discriminatory acts. Experts and former police officers say a lack of veteran presence among patrol officers can lead to problems.
Patrol officers at Station 39 had average of 4 years' experience in 2026, down from 7 in 2021

As Montreal police manage the fallout of back-to-back scandals involving recent recruits, newly obtained internal data reveals a drop in seniority levels at the station at the centre of a major scandal this summer.
Earlier this month, an officer with just three years' experience was suspended after allegedly urinating on homeless people while on the job.
That followed the dismantling in June of a 16-member patrol unit at Station 39 in Montréal-Nord after allegations of racial discrimination and misconduct.
In the aftermath of those revelations, Montreal police Chief Fady Dagher told CBC News that many of the officers involved were young men with less than five years of experience on the force.

Now, staffing statistics obtained by CBC News through an access-to-information request reveal an overall decline in the level of experience among Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) patrol officers in the past five years at Station 39.
The precinct oversees Montréal-Nord, a racially diverse borough with a long history of documented racial profiling and fraught relations between residents and police.

items: Montreal police officer who allegedly urinated on homeless people faces ethics probe

blocks.text: Front-line neighbourhood patrol officers, known as agents de quartier, averaged just 4.2 years of service in 2026, compared with 7.1 five years earlier.
The demographic breakdown shows overall average seniority at the station dropped from 10.6 years in 2021 to 8.5 in 2026. Patrol supervisors, meanwhile, average 18.7 years' experience in 2026.
The SPVM said the drop in experience is not unique to Station 39, but part of a citywide demographic shift driven by a wave of retirements.
In a written statement to CBC News, police said it has renewed 35 per cent of its personnel over the past five years, hiring about 1,000 new recruits in the last three years alone to fill the void.

Police also pushed back against the claim that young officers are left without veteran oversight on the street. All new arrivals undergo a 15-week integration program where they are paired with specially trained coaching officers to guide them through their first months on the job, the statement said.
The SPVM also said that supervisors regularly go out in the field with their patrol officers, "particularly for major calls requiring an incident commander to take charge."
Why veteran oversight matters, according to experts

Still, the data points to a concerning dynamic in policing, where veteran officers are often distant from the daily realities of street patrol, according to Victor Armony, a sociology professor at Université du Québec à Montréal who studies policing and racial profiling.
Top-down directives from police leadership, he added, won't necessarily reach rookie patrol groups who have become "in a way, autonomous."
Armony also cautioned against the assumption that a younger generation of officers, raised with modern diversity training, will naturally rid the force of discrimination.

"This notion that older police officers are more sexist or more closed to diversity while young people have grown up already in a world where you accept everybody for who they are — that's naive, that's reductive," he said in an interview.

items: SPVM chief faces big questions over police racism investigation
Montreal police allegedly cut locs from people's hair. Here's the anti-Black history behind that

blocks.text: Instead, he pointed to the dismantled unit at Station 39 as a symptom of a broader structural failure, where a lack of experienced oversight allowed alleged misconduct to go unchecked.
According to a separate batch of documents obtained by The Canadian Press, a "radicalized" subculture formed among the ranks of officers at the station.
"If you have a good organizational structure ... the bad apples will be evident more quickly than when you leave them to fester," Armony said.
"It's unbelievable that they could be there for so long doing the things they have allegedly been doing, and no one saw."
Fady Dagher, Montreal's police chief, said he will take steps to improve the culture within the SPVM. (Ivanoh Demers/Radio-Canada)
Police defend supervision, training
Police have since submitted evidence to Quebec prosecutors regarding the June misconduct allegations at Station 39.
Asked if a lack of direct supervision on the ground allowed a toxic culture to take root, the SPVM said it is too early to draw conclusions.
"The investigations are ongoing, so it seems premature to comment on this issue," the SPVM said, adding that the "results will tell us if there was a lack of supervision."
The SPVM also pointed to its Immersion MTL program, launched in 2023, which requires recruits to spend four weeks without uniforms or weapons interacting with community groups.
A total of 747 officers have completed the training so far and the feedback has been positive, helping recruits understand the realities of the city, the statement said.
Montreal police described ‘radicalized’ subculture among Station 39 officers, internal documents say
Alain Babineau, a former RCMP staff sergeant, said police officers naturally want to move on from patrol work.
"Front-line policing is the toughest job in policing. It's thankless and dangerous," said Babineau, racial profiling director with the advocacy group Red Coalition.
"You should do this for three, five years and then move on to something else because it's very taxing on the individual. And there lies the importance of very good supervision at that level."

Yet because veteran officers have priority when choosing their assignments, many opt out of working on patrol in a demanding post such as Station 39, said Minh-Tri Truong, a retired commander with the SPVM.
This creates a dangerous cycle where rookies are being mentored by peers who only have a few months on the job themselves, Truong told CBC.
"In the long term, this police officer moves to another station and he has five years of experience on paper ... but he just learned from somebody who had six months."

items: Montreal approves motion — with amendments — for police chief to appear before council

blocks.text: Referring to the situation at Station 39, Truong suggested that "when you have a more senior officer, maybe those situations have less of a risk to happen."
The SPVM disputes the idea that veterans are avoiding the precinct.
The statement described Station 39 as a "popular assignment," noting that when it asked for volunteers to replace the dismantled patrol unit in June, it received a large number of applications.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Benjamin Shingler is an investigative reporter based in Montreal. He previously worked at The Canadian Press, CTV and the New Brunswick Telegraph-Journal. You can email story ideas or tips to montrealinvestigates@cbc.ca, or reach out on Signal at @bshingler.67

Violent protests broke out against a proposed hydroelectric project in Arunachal Pradesh on Monday in Daporijo town.

articles.title: Major Chinese brands drop Mbappé as backlash grows over Mao joke
articles.summary: He allegedly said his "favourite meme" is "the one where they put my face on a Chinese dictator".

blocks.text: Even China's foreign ministry has weighed in, with spokesperso Lin Jian: "We have noted the relevant reports. Words and deeds that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with opposition from all sectors of Chinese society."
Neither Mbappé nor the The Bridge have commented on this yet.

It's unclear when the interview was broadcast but Chinese football forum Dongqiudi drew attention to the comments on Monday night in a statement, saying they were "inappropriate" and "hurt the feelings of Chinese people".

A backlash quickly ensued online, with some users criticising Mbappé – who is hugely popular in China and has big endorsements - of "profiting from the Chinese market yet making remarks that offend the Chinese public".
"International public figures, in particular, should show greater respect and sensitivity, as national sentiment must never be taken lightly," read another comment on Weibo.

Mao founded Communist China in 1949 and ruled through tumultuous decades in the 1960s and 1970s. His attempt at rapid industrialisation, which he called the Great Leap Forward, led to a famine that killed tens of millions. Then came the Cultural Revolution: a violent purge of anyone seen as a threat to Communism, which included Chinese intellectuals, landowners, artists and often rivals within the Party.

His death in 1976 brought a new era for China, which began to open its doors to the global economy. Even as the country moved away from Mao's rule, he continued to be hailed by the Chinese Communist Party as a national icon whose legacy was beyond reproach.
Given how Mao is regarded to this day in China, the may seem unsurprising to many.

The backlash is still growing. Chinese state broadcaster, CCTV, is suspending La Liga matches, according to The Paper. And some reports claim t 's state broadcaster CCTV's news apps no longer have content related to the French striker.
The Chinese brands have not explicitly said why they were terminating the contract but referred to hurt sentiments.
The country's largest dairy producer, Mengniu, said it "firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any words or actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people".
Drinks giant Dongpeng, said: "Our company firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any behaviour that offends national sentiments."
Given brands have not mentioned the controversial clip, some users on social media are also asking what exactly Mbappé had said or done that was offensive.

Mbappé, who made his debut for Real Madrid in August 2024, has been nicknamed "the dictator" in the football world because of his influence and control over club and international football operations.
In 2024, he sued a French influencer and kebab shop owner for using his name in the description of one of the shop's sandwiches. Some say the incident reinforced his "dictator" portrayal.
The nickname has also made Mbappé the subject of many memes online.

France team-mate Ousmane Dembele jumped on the trend during the 2026 World Cup by calling Mbappé Mobut – a reference to Mobutu Sese Seko, the dictator who ruled the Democratic Republic of Congo, formerly Zaire, for three decades.

In an interview with France Football in September, Mbappé acknowledged the light-heartedness behind many of these memes, but said they "sometimes reveals a lack of political and human awareness among people".
"There's a side that's a bit less funny, because we know the damage people like that have caused throughout history.
"Being compared to people who murder others, or who have made millions upon millions of people miserable... I don't think I've done that in my life," he had said.

articles.title: Melting glaciers in Dolomites reveal cache of first world war munitions
articles.summary:
Italian army removes and defuses 250 explosives encased in ice for more than 100 years after hikers’ sightings

A significant cache of unexploded bombs from the first world war emerged this…

blocks.text: A significant cache of unexploded bombs from the first world war emerged this summer from rapidly retreating glaciers in the Dolomites, the Italian army has said.
The devices, which included Italian artillery shells and French mortar bombs, were removed and defused by the army’s Julia Alpine brigade, according to a statement.
The weapons originated from the white war, a battle between the Austro-Hungarian army and Italian troops across treacherous and bitterly cold terrain between 1915 and 1918.

blocks.caption: Soldiers from Italian army’s Julia Alpine brigade at work. Photograph: Julia Alpine brigade

blocks.text: More than a century later, hikers reported several sightings of bombs during the summer, mostly in the area of Canal San Bovo in the Primiero Valley in eastern Trentino. The soldiers then conducted an extensive sweep there and across other high-altitude and glacier locations in the Trentino Alto Adige region of the Dolomites.

They recovered and neutralised 250 explosives, including “18 Italian 75mm artillery shells and 37 Thevetot mortar shells – a French-made device that was also supplied to the Italian royal army during the first world war”, the Julia Alpine brigade.
It is not the first time that relics of the white war have emerged from melting glaciers, whose retreat has accelerated over more than decade.

blocks.caption: A soldier with some of the munitions recovered.  Photograph: Julia Alpine brigade

blocks.text: “It is very much a consequence of global heating,” said Stefano Morosini, a professor at the University of Bergamo and the coordinator of heritage projects at Stelvio national park, where some of the explosives were also found.

“In recent years, at the end of each summer, these dangerous artefacts emerge and each year there is a higher number. They have been conserved by the ice for more than 100 years. Some had already exploded but many hadn’t, so now when they re-emerge, they are very, very dangerous.”
The advice to hikers and mountaineers is to “never touch any type of explosive device you might find, regardless of where it is located” and to promptly report any discovery to police.

Fought mainly in the Dolomites of Trentino Alto-Adige and the Alps of the Lombardy region, the white war was a period of history frozen in time until the 1990s, when global heating started to reveal an assortment of perfectly preserved relics, including weapons, sledges, letters and diaries.
after newsletter promotion

A wooden barracks that had been dug into a cave on the top of Mount Scorluzzo, a 3,095-metre (10,154ft) peak overlooking the Stelvio pass, reappeared in 2015 after the ice which had sealed it off for almost a century completely melted.

The shelter had been hastily locked up when the first world war ended in November 1918, and the soldiers abandoned most of their belongings. Beds made of straw as well as clothes, lanterns, newspapers, postcards, coins, and tinned food were found well preserved inside.
A white war museum to host the relics is scheduled to open in Bormio in June 2027.
The white war is thought to have claimed more than a million lives, although the majority of soldiers were believed to have been killed by avalanches, falling down mountains or hypothermia.
Dozens of corpses, some still in their uniforms, have emerged from the melting ice over the past 15 years.
The relatives of an Italian soldier were able to bury him in 2017 after documents revealing his identity were found with his body on Presena glacier.
Morosini said the intense summer heat was making access to the glaciers in the Dolomites less safe. Eleven people died when a huge mass of the Marmolada glacier broke off in 2022.
“It is becoming more and more impossible to access the glaciers during the summer because of the very long heatwave at high altitude,” he said.
“If you come to the area, you can see how fast the glaciers are retreating and how strong the impact of climate change is.”
