blocks.text: Closing summary

items: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the Brazilian president, has vowed that dictatorship and fascism will never return to Brazil after winning a historic fourth term in power by defeating his far-right opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro. “This is God’s work – and it’s thanks to all of you,” Lula told tens of thousands of supporters who had gathered in central São Paulo in the early hours of Monday to celebrate his dramatic election comeback.

A few hours earlier, Lula pulled off the most stunning political fightback in modern Brazilian history, bouncing back from a first-round defeat in early October to trounce Bolsonaro by more than 4m votes in the runoff. Never, since the return of democracy after the 1964-85 military regime, had the first-round loser managed to win the second vote.

However, Bolsonaro rejected the result, following in the footsteps of his father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who refused to concede after losing the 2022 election to Lula and was later convicted of plotting a coup. He called Lula’s victory “sacanagem”, a Portuguese word that roughly translates as “bullshit”.

The scale of Bolsonaro’s loss, with the senator trailing Lula by over 4 ​million votes, makes it unlikely his efforts to annul the vote will succeed, analysts said. Less than ‌35,000 votes, or some 0.03% of the total, ‌were cast in the extra two hours of voting ordered by the Supreme Court, according to an analysis of electoral records by Insper professor Pedro Burgos.

Political leaders and governments from across the spectrum were quick to recognise Lula’s victory. Mexico’s leftwing president, Claudia Sheinbaum, tweeted: “Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won.” Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, wrote: “The global progressive resurgence has just begun.”

French president Emmanuel Macron said France and Brazil had “much to build together,” while European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen said “democracy and multilateralism have won in Brazil.” The Kremlin welcomed Lula’s re-election and praised him for his contribution ‌to bilateral ties and to BRICS. Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy congratulated the leftist leader on “remarkable election results” and said he looked forward to expanding cooperation.

Rampant selling tore through financial markets at the shock result, as investors reversed positions that had largely been built around expectations of a Bolsonaro victory. Brazil’s currency tumbled over 11% against the US dollar in early spot trading, one of its biggest daily declines on record, while the benchmark Bovespa stock ⁠index was down more than 15% in its largest daily percentage drop since 1998.

blocks.text: Nearly three million more people voted in the second round of the Brazilian election than the first.
Here is a graphic that shows how that compares with previous elections in the country:

blocks.caption: Tiago Rogero

blocks.text: Tiago Rogero

Brazilian newspaper Folha de S.Paulo published an analysis showing that only 34,330 votes, or 0.03% of the total, were cast after the original 5pm closing time, an insignificant number compared with the 4.4 million-vote margin by which president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defeated his opponent.

The decision to extend voting until 7pm so that voters who had been unable to access the mandatory free public transport could cast their ballots is at the heart of far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro’s attempt to have the election annulled.

However, the president of the electoral court, justice Kassio Nunes Marques, has already said the extension did not affect the result and, like the leaders of other Brazilian institutions including the supreme court and congress, has recognised Lula’s re-election.

So few votes were actually cast because, as the decision to extend voting hours came minutes after 5pm, the vast majority of electronic voting machines had already been closed and could not be reopened.

The analysis was carried out at Folha de S.Paulo’s request by data journalist and university professor Pedro Burgos, who believes most of the 34,000 votes cast after 5pm were from voters who were already queuing when the original voting period ended – meaning they would have been able to vote even without the extension.
The British foreign secretary has described Lula’s victory as “a historic win for the global progressive movement” as he offered his congratulations.
Ed Miliband wrote on X:

double quotation markCongratulations to @LulaOficial on his re-election. Together, our two governments have promoted shared values of democracy, social justice and climate action since 2024 and look forward to continuing to do so. His victory is a historic win for the global progressive movement.

We reported earlier that the Kremlin had sent a warm message to Lula on his re-election, with Valdimir Putin’s spokesperson Dmitry Peskov saying it was “welcomed”, praising his efforts on the “development of bilateral relations” between the two nations.
Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has also commented. He said:

double quotation markFor us in Ukraine, it is important that Brazil remains active in international affairs and continues to contribute to the effective protection of human rights, the rights of peoples, and the rights of states. We thank Brazil for its unwavering support for Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. We look forward to expanding our cooperation.

Dr Marco Vieira, associate professor in international relations at the University of Birmingham in England, has said there are three distinct reasons why the world should pay attention to the election result in Brazil. He said:

double quotation markFirst, Lula’s victory reinforces Brazil’s role in spearheading efforts to protect the Amazon rainforest, with clear implications for global climate patterns, food production and the rights of Indigenous populations living in the region. Second, Lula will now face a major challenge as the leader of South America’s largest economy and one of the region’s most important powers resisting what Trump has called his “Donroe Doctrine”, a policy of expanding US influence and asserting US dominance in the western Hemisphere. Third, Brazil is likely to continue its international activism through forums such as BRICS and the G20, positioning itself as a leading voice in debates over global governance reform and the defence of multilateral institutions. In a context of growing global uncertainty, the certainty of Lula leading Brazil for the next four years provides an important source of support for other middle powers seeking to rebuild trust in multilateralism and peaceful cooperation.

blocks.caption: Tom Phillips

blocks.text: Tom Phillips
Tom Phillips is the Guardian’s Latin America correspondent
I’ve been speaking to Brazil’s former environment minister, the world-renowned environmentalist Marina Silva, here in São Paulo.

A few days ago she told me that if Flávio Bolsonaro were to be elected president he would seek to finish the “perverse project” of rampant rainforest destruction initiated by his jailed far-right father.
On Sunday night Silva was in a far more upbeat mood as she arrived at the hall where Lula was celebrating his election triumph with hundreds of ecstatic supporters.
“My heart is happy and filled with gratitude to God and the Brazilian people,” she told me.

“The thing I most feared was that our Indigenous territories would be invaded again [under another Bolsonaro government]. Now, I am certain that they will be preserved and that there is no risk of illegal miners returning to destroy these populations,” Silva said.

blocks.caption: Brazil's former minister of the environment Marina Silva. Photograph: Adriano Machado/Reuters

blocks.text: Jair Bolsonaro spent his 2019-22 presidency stripping away environmental and Indigenous protests and was nicknamed “Captain Chainsaw” because of the devastation inflicted on the environment under his watch.

After beating Bolsonaro in the 2022 election, Lula launched a major crackdown to evict illegal miners from Indigenous lands and a broader environmental offensive across the Amazon that cut deforestation to its lowest levels since the late 80s.
Those efforts will now continue.
Summary of the day so far …

items: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the Brazilian president, has staged a dramatic election fightback, defeating his far-right opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, to claim a historic fourth term in power.
However, soon after Brazil’s electoral authority confirmed Lula’s victory, Bolsonaro refused to concede defeat and asked for the results to be annulled.

Following in the footsteps of his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, who four years ago also refused to acknowledge his defeat to Lula – before attempting a coup and being convicted for it – the senator cited a supreme court justice’s decision to extend voting hours as the alleged reason.

His claim apears to be making little headway, with president of the electoral court, justice Kassio Nunes Marques, and the heads of the supreme court, the lower house and the senate all recognising the result and congratulating the incumbent on his re-election.

The unexpected result has caused some market turmoil, with Brazil’s National Treasury cancelling ⁠auctions of inflation-linked ⁠and fixed-rate government ​bonds, the São Paulo stock exchange halting trading, and Brazil’s real weakened ⁠12.2% ⁠against ​the US ⁠dollar.

The Kremlin has welcomed Lula’s election victory, saying the leftist president had done “a lot” to develop ties with Russia. Numerous other world leaders have congratulated Lula for his dramatic election win, but so far Donald Trump has remained silent.
You can find the full election results here.

Brazil’s National Treasury said in ⁠a ⁠statement on ​Monday it has canceled ⁠the conventional auctions of inflation-linked ⁠and fixed-rate government ​bonds scheduled ‌for ‌27 October and ‌29 October, Reuters reports.
Reuters reports that the currency market speculators have had their say on the election result – Brazil’s real weakened ⁠12.2% ⁠against ​the US ⁠dollar in spot trading ⁠early ​on Monday.

articles.title: German police probe cruise ship captain after Bremerhaven collision
articles.summary: A three-ship collision has led to the cancellation of a cruise and expensive damages. Shipyard repairs are needed, and further cruises could be affected.

image.caption: Police are investigating whether the captain breached his duty of care during the ship's departureImage: Sina Schuldt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: German police are investigating the captain of the Mein Schiff 3 cruise liner after it collided with two container ships in Bremerhaven.
The collision caused damage estimated to be in the millions of euros and forced the cancellation of a 20-day Canary Islands cruise, with further voyages potentially affected.
Why are police investigating the captain?

A police spokesperson said proceedings over a possible administrative offense had been opened to establish whether the captain breached his duty of care. Police have not specified the suspected lapse.
Broadcaster RTL reported that investigators spoke to the captains of all three vessels overnight into Monday.
How did the collision happen?
Tugboats were helping the nearly fully booked cruise ship leave the northern German port on Sunday evening when a gust of wind pushed it toward two moored container ships, police said.
The liner was carrying 2,428 passengers and 922 crew members. Nobody was injured, and none of the vessels took on water.
The larger container ship suffered substantial damage, with several meters of its port side torn open and container guides deformed. The smaller vessel sustained minor damage.
The cruise ship was also significantly damaged. Photographs showed damage to its lifeboats and bridge.

blocks.caption: The collision forced the cancellation of a 20-day Canary Islands cruise, with police investigating the captainImage: Sina Schuldt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: All damage was several meters above the waterline. The liner returned to the cruise terminal after the collision.
Could more cruises be canceled?
Technical experts boarded the ship shortly after the accident and determined that shipyard repairs were necessary, operator TUI Cruises said.

The company called canceling the Canary Islands voyage "the only responsible decision," saying passenger and crew safety had "highest priority." Passengers were initially allowed to remain aboard while the company arranged assistance.
It remained unclear whether other voyages planned for this year could go ahead.
The collision initially caused no disruption to other harbor traffic.

articles.title: Israel and the US are both going to the polls - the consequences will be global
articles.summary: The next fortnight sees two elections on different continents. The outcomes will shape geopolitics and the global economy, writes James Landale

blocks.text: Image source, Getty
By
Diplomatic correspondentReporting fromJerusalem

blocks.caption: James Landale

blocks.text: In the next week, two sets of elections will be held on two continents, the outcomes of which could have profound consequences for the world.
By a fluke of electoral timetabling, millions of voters around 6,000 miles apart will unite in exercising their democratic rights within days of each other.
Voters in Israel go to the polls on Tuesday to elect a new parliament; a week later, voters in the United States will elect a new Congress.
A former speaker of that Congress, Tip O'Neill, may have once said that "all politics is local". But the consequences of these elections will undoubtedly be global.
For these elections are not just proximate, they are intertwined.
The future governance of Israel will have a lasting impact on the Middle East and wars raging across the region.
And any change in the electoral map of America could shape not just those wars but also the future of the global economy.
Between the two there is a physical connection: the lobby group Republicans Overseas Israel estimates about half a million Israelis with American passports can vote in both polls.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has highlighted his alliance with US President Donald Trump - including in this Likud party election billboard in Tel Aviv

blocks.text: Image source, EPA/Shutterstock
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has highlighted his alliance with US President Donald Trump - including in this Likud party election billboard in Tel Aviv

Marc Zell, the group's chairman, said these electors could influence tight races in the US, such as the Michigan senatorial contest, in which he estimated 10,000 absentee ballots would be cast from Israel. "They can really make a difference," he told the BBC.

But the policy connection is perhaps deeper - and most acute regarding the US-Israeli war on Iran. The massive aerial attack, which began in February, destroyed many military targets and killed much of Iran's leadership. But it failed to overthrow the regime which hit back hard across the Gulf and seized control of the Strait of Hormuz and the energy that flowed through it.
The Iran question
The sheer fact of the elections has already shaped decision-making.
Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has used the campaign to talk up the possibility of launching a fresh attack on Iran.
He has made new claims – without providing evidence – about Iran's nuclear threat, insisting again the Islamic regime must be overthrown.
His aim: to shore up his reputation as a security leader, which took such a battering after the deadly 7 October Hamas-led attacks on Israel.
US President Donald Trump has added to the speculation of renewed attacks on Iran by endorsing Netanyahu's re-election campaign, saying both men should "soon finish the job" in Iran.

Yet for all the sabre-rattling, there have also been contradictory reports that Trump intervened to restrain Netanyahu from attacking Iran before polling day, fearing a fresh spike in energy prices would remind US voters of his unpopular war.

blocks.caption: Image caption, President Trump has been campaigning on behalf of Republican congressional candidates, including in Michigan on Sunday, where there's a tight Senate race

blocks.text: Image source, REUTERS/Jonathan Ernst
President Trump has been campaigning on behalf of Republican congressional candidates, including in Michigan on Sunday, where there's a tight Senate race

So might an attack on Iran, then, be delayed until after the elections? Israel's media is full of speculation Netanyahu could try to engineer his survival by attacking Iran as caretaker prime minister after the election.

He would argue, so the theory goes, for a government of national unity – involving him – rather than a coalition between opposition parties. Netanyahu has long been seen as a great survivor of Israeli politics. If he were to lose power, he would face an official inquiry into his actions before the October 7 attacks and renewed legal proceedings involving allegations of corruption.

So real is this speculation that Netanyahu's rival, the former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has already ruled out joining any unity government. Like all mainstream Israeli politicians, Eisenkot sees Iran as an existential threat to Israel and supports military action against the Islamic regime. But he has explicitly warned against escalating the war for political purposes.
'Legacy mode'

Certainly, Trump may be more willing to attack Iran after the midterms if he is unconstrained electorally and hoping to extract himself from the war with one more push. Some analysts believe Iran is so economically weak from the war and economic sanctions that a fresh round of military strikes might encourage Iranians to overthrow the regime. Others see this as yet more wishful thinking. It is a strategy that has repeatedly failed, but still has currency in Washington.
"After the midterms, he will be in legacy mode," one well-placed Western diplomat told me. "He will want to show agency on anything that is not the quagmire at home."

In Israel there is a broad consensus across most parties about the threat from and the need to constrain Iran. But if voters elect a new government, they might have a prime minister with less political and personal investment in fresh attacks.

In those circumstances, Trump has suggested his thinking may change, too. "If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi [a nickname for Netanyahu], America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," he wrote on social media.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Netanyahu has used this year's election campaign to talk up the possibility of a fresh attack on Iran

blocks.text: Netanyahu has used this year's election campaign to talk up the possibility of a fresh attack on Iran

Little wonder policymakers in Tehran have been following US opinion polls as closely as any analyst inside the Washington beltway. The risk, of course, is that any post-electoral strikes would plunge the Middle East into fresh chaos if Iran were to retaliate hard.
Publicly and privately, Iranian officials have threatened to hit airports, pipelines, undersea cables, energy facilities, desalination plants as well as US bases and warships.
Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, wrote in the Financial Times that new attacks would put "civilian lives and the wellbeing of all regional states and the global economy at great risk".
It's the economy

The two elections again intertwine around the global economy. Affordability and cost of living have dominated campaigning for the midterms, issues made worse by Trump's war that raised prices as Iran choked the flow of energy through the Strait of Hormuz.

The economy is also an election issue in Israel, where voters face high costs and low wages. But here, too, the war plays its part with soaring defence spending putting even more pressure on the public finances.

Trump has sought to appease voters ahead of the midterms. He has lifted sanctions on Russia, hoping in vain that by importing diesel from Moscow, prices might fall significantly. He has been taking a tough line with Ukraine, calling on its leadership to make concessions in the hope – also so far in vain – of claiming a foreign policy victory.

But Republican ire at his controversial strategy is growing. Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina, a frequent critic of Trump, told CBS News: "If the President wants to actually bring down energy prices, he can do it by solving the Iran problem, not by doing a solid [favour] for Vladimir Putin."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Early voting has already started in many US states for next month's midterms

blocks.text: Image source, Chris Torres / EPA/Shutterstock
Early voting has already started in many US states for next month's midterms

One consequence of the Iran war – along with Israel's military operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank – is that traditional bipartisan support in the US has fractured. Abdul El-Sayed, the left-wing Democratic candidate for the Senate in Michigan, campaigns on cutting military aid to Israel. "An ally that takes your money, to push you into wars you shouldn't be fighting, is not an ally," he told ABC News.

The US and Israel initially attacked Iran to destroy its ballistic missiles, degrade its nuclear capability, weaken its support for proxy militias and even oust the entire regime. Since then its war aims have changed to reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

Brad Lander, a Democratic congressional candidate in New York who also sits on the left of his party, chose even to travel to the West Bank only days before polling. He helped Palestinians harvest olives and was briefly detained by Israeli forces, all grist to his social media electoral mill. In the history of US politics, this is not normal. Even Netanyahu is warning that Israel may in future have to survive without a US security blanket.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The leader of Israel's Yashar party, Gadi Eisenkot, has ruled out joining a unity government after the elections

blocks.text: Image source, Abir Sultan Credit / EPA/Shutterstock
The leader of Israel's Yashar party, Gadi Eisenkot, has ruled out joining a unity government after the elections

Of course, if Israel's prime minister were to lose, his departure would end a scratchy bromance that has seen Trump blow hot and cold. Last week the president called his Israeli counterpart a "great warrior prime minister". During the summer, he said Netanyahu was "effing crazy". A new Israeli leader would have to forge a new relationship with an outgoing US president, a very different dynamic.

If the Democrats were to win greater control in Congress, that might place some check on blanket US support for Israel. Congress has traditional powers that it can use to restrain military spending. It could also cut military aid to Israel. But as president, Trump would retain significant executive power – and a veto – to continue prosecuting the conflict as he saw fit.

The decision by Israel and the US to go to war with Iran earlier this year transformed the global economy and international geopolitics. The choices voters in both nations make in coming days may shape where the world goes next.

articles.title: 10 percent of pupils in Grades 1-3 are struggling readers
articles.summary: Ten percent of Grades 1 to 3 learners are struggling readers, according to the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM2).

blocks.text: October 27, 2026 | 12:00am
MANILA, Philippines — Ten percent of Grades 1 to 3 learners are struggling readers, according to the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM2).
Based on the End-of-School-Year 2025-2026 assessment, EDCOM2 said 10 percent of the 5,127,670 learners covered were still struggling to read.

The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao recorded the highest proportion of struggling readers at 25.5 percent, followed by Soccsksargen at 17.7 percent and the Zamboanga Peninsula at 14.7 percent, according to the EDCOM2 Early Childhood Dashboard.
Bicol ranked fourth at 12 percent, followed by the Davao region at 11.7 percent and Mimaropa at 11.3 percent.

The Negros Island Region and Central Visayas both recorded 10.4 percent, while Caraga had 10 percent, Ilocos 9.4 percent, Northern Mindanao 9.3 percent, Cagayan Valley 8.6 percent, Western Visayas 8.2 percent, Central Luzon 7.9 percent, Eastern Visayas 7.2 percent and Calabarzon 6.7 percent.
The Cordillera Administrative Region and the National Capital Region recorded the lowest proportions of struggling readers at 5.3 percent each.
In Davao del Sur, struggling readers accounted for 9.5 percent of learners, while Davao City recorded 9.3 percent, EDCOM2 said.
Meanwhile, only 25 percent of senior high school students in Davao City were considered independent readers based on the Senior High School Learning Needs Assessment results for EOSY 2025-2026.
The EDCOM2 early childhood dashboard consolidates local data on child nutrition, early literacy and Child Development Center coverage to support targeted early childhood interventions.
Social media

In a separate development, Education Secretary Sonny Angara yesterday backed efforts to regulate social media use among minors, saying the government cannot control children’s exposure to online platforms at home.

Angara’s statement came after the Senate passed on third and final reading a bill requiring high-risk digital services to suspend, restrict, disable or remove accounts owned, operated or used by individuals under 18.

“The proposed bill is important. I know that there are debates on what is the right age, etc.,” Angara said after attending the Comprehensive Media Program for Children and Its Role in Policy Making summit in Quezon City.

The proposed Safe Media Access and Responsible Technology for Kids in Digital Spaces (SMART KIDS) Act seeks to prohibit minors from accessing high-risk digital services, including Roblox and GoreBox, online platforms where vulnerable young people are reportedly groomed into committing violent acts.

“But for us, we can’t control everything. We prohibit the use of those apps in schools. But when it comes to their own homes, we can’t control it. That’s why we appreciate those kinds of social media regulations. And it’s proven that if children use apps for a long time, their depression and anxiety will increase,” Angara said.

The proposed ban does not cover email services, private messaging services, online gaming services not primarily used for social networking, educational platforms, news services and professional collaboration services.

articles.title: How 'Lula's Army' WhatsApp channel helped turn Brazil election around
articles.summary: Millions joined a 'Lula's Army' channel that helped to transform online enthusiasm into real-world mobilisation.
articles.byline: Julia Braun, Rute Pina, Luiz Fernando Toledo

blocks.text: The emergence of Lula's Army convinced many supporters that Brazil's left had finally found a way to compete in a digital arena. The shift was particularly significant because social media has played a central role in Brazilian politics since Jair Bolsonaro's 2018 election victory, when WhatsApp networks became a defining feature of political campaigning.

Lula's Army messages often included ready-made templates for followers to share with friends and family. Each one assigned supporters a specific task aimed at boosting Lula's visibility on social media.
Janones frequently instructed his "troops" to "blow up" the latest campaign video or help a new hashtag "take off".
"Guys, urgent!", "Don't go to sleep yet", "No food before the mission!", and "I have one more task before you're dismissed", were some of the instructions.
On the eve of the election, the congressman also hosted a 24-hour live event - dubbed the "turnaround livestream" - even as polls continued to suggest a victory for Bolsonaro.

The tactic worked, despite worries by some members of the Workers' Party that Janones's often-confrontational style on social media could undermine the more moderate image they hoped to project for Lula.
In his victory speech, Lula referred to Janones as "our General" and thanked him for "raising the morale of our troops every day".
Measuring the electoral impact of online mobilisation, however, is notoriously difficult.

While Lula's allies credit Lula's Army with helping fuel the comeback, political scientists caution that it is impossible to determine how many votes, if any, were directly influenced by the WhatsApp operation.
Political scientist Denilde Holzhacker argues that a shift in Lula's campaign strategy was key to his comeback.
Rather than relying solely on online engagement, she says the Workers' Party candidate succeeded in connecting digital campaigning with grassroots mobilisation on the ground.

According to Holzhacker, the campaign intensified local efforts and adapted its messaging - linking a Bolsonaro victory with concerns about potential changes to social programmes and the loss of rights.

"It was to Lula's credit that he recognised his own weakness and completely changed his style," she says. "And Janones managed to do something that had seemed unthinkable for Brazil's left - dominate social media."
By contrast, Holzhacker argues that Flávio Bolsonaro entered the run-off overly confident of victory and failed to communicate his message to his supporters as effectively.
Sociologist and political scientist Mayra Goulart, a professor at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, also cautions against attributing Lula's comeback solely to social media.
"It was a combination of social media and street-level mobilisation," she says. "The physical world enabled a form of mobilisation capable of reducing abstention and persuading undecided voters."
In her view, Lula's supporters succeeded in turning online enthusiasm into real-world political engagement.
"Those committed to Lula's victory worked to bring people together and persuade them to vote," Goulart says.
She argues that the effort not only helped increase turnout but could also prove valuable for Lula's next administration.

"I believe this collective effort was an important learning experience and will prove valuable for a government that still faces many battles ahead. It not only helped reduce abstention, but also converted a significant number of undecided voters."
Lula himself suggested that the mobilisation behind his comeback could shape the way he governs in the years ahead.
In his victory speech, he said the election had taught him many lessons and pledged to change the way Brazil is governed.
"We are going to give people a greater say in decision-making, and digital communication will play a much bigger role in my government."

articles.title: What Germany thinks of carmaker Audi's $4 billion deal with Trump
articles.summary: The luxury carmaker is set to open its first factory in the United States — a move Trump credits to his tariffs. DW examines the German reaction amid a massive auto industry cull at home.

image.caption: Audi hopes that its plans to build SUVs in the US can revive the company's fortunesImage: AFP

blocks.text: 1. What is Audi's $4 billion US investment plan?
US President Donald Trump announced the investment on Saturday, during a campaign rally in Georgia, a key battleground state for his Republican Party in the midterm elections next week.
Audi quickly confirmed the plan, saying it would build its first US factory near Macon, Georgia, costing around $4 billion (€3.6 billion) and creating some 4,500 jobs.
The German automaker said construction would begin next year, with a planned annual production of up to 200,000 vehicles due to start in the early 2030s.
The firm plans to build premium SUVs for the US market at the plant, marking a "long-term commitment" to what it said was "one of the world's most important premium markets."
The US investment comes as German automakers face unprecedented pressure from China, rising costs and two conflicts.

Backed by huge government subsidies, Chinese rivals have stolen a march in the transition to electric vehicles (EVs), scaling up production of new models that are fast gaining market share in a crowded global auto market.
BMW, Mercedes-Benz and Audi's parent company, Volkswagen— the world's second-largest automaker — have all issued profit warnings in recent months as margins come under pressure.

They've also announced major cost-cutting. VW is preparing to axe up to 100,000 jobs by 2030, while Audi's factory in Neckarsulm, which has around 15,000 staff, is one of four plants at risk of closure.
2. Why is Audi investing in US car production?
Trump credited his 15% tariffs on European-made vehicles for Audi's investment, saying it "would not have happened without tariffs."
While the commitment does feed into Trump's plan to bring manufacturing back to the United States from abroad, Audi said it was making the huge outlay for growth and resilience.
“We have much greater ambitions for Audi in America," said the carmaker's CEO Gernot Döllner, who appeared alongside Trump at the Republican's campaign rally.

"The United States is one of the world's most important premium markets, and we have not yet realized our full potential. We are determined to change that ... This is about building a stronger Audi business in America — not only about building a factory," he said.
However, Trump's tariffs have undoubtedly added to the automaker's woes.
Audi, which currently exports to the US market from Europe and Mexico, said the additional costs amounted to about €1.2 billion ($1.3 billion) last year.
With more than 160,000 vehicles sold, Audi's US sales last year fell 16%, amid intense competition and after Trump scrapped subsidies on electric vehicles in its second-biggest market.
By building a US factory, Audi should be able to avoid or reduce Trump's tariffs, industry analysts say.
EU to weaken combustion engine ban amid industry pressure
3. What is the reaction in Germany amid huge cuts in the domestic auto sector?
There's been fierce criticism of the deal due to the severe pressure facing German automakers and because the new US investment could mean further job losses at home.
Much of the criticism focused on Döllner's rally appearance alongside Trump.
The center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD)'s transport policy spokesperson Isabel Cademartori described it as campaign assistance for an autocrat who is waging a trade war against Germany.
"This is a disgrace, especially considering the history of the Volkswagen Group," she stated, referring to the party's links with Adolf Hitler's Nazi party during World War II.
Christiane Benner, president of the powerful IG Metall union, labeled the rally appearance as "extremely embarrassing, politically unacceptable and not worthy of the company."
VW works council chief Daniela Cavallo went further, saying Döllner had let himself be turned "into a puppet in [Trump's] propaganda show."

blocks.caption: Audi's CEO Döllner (right) has been strongly criticized for appearing alongside Donald Trump at a midterms campaign rallyImage: Edgar Su/REUTERS

blocks.text: Cavallo, however, noted that the US plant could make sense from a business perspective, as VW needs to grow its market share there.
An Audi spokesperson defended the US investment, saying it was "not a decision against Germany, but rather a step toward strengthening our global competitiveness."
Manfred Döss, chairman of Audi's supervisory board, insisted the automaker's future cannot be secured by cost-cutting and efficiency alone.
"We need the courage to invest, to seize new opportunities and to make decisions that will shape our company for decades to come," he added.
4. Will Audi's investment help Trump in the US midterms?
The announcement certainly appears timed to coincide with the US midterm elections on November 3.
Voters will decide whether the Republicans or Democrats hold the balance of power in Congress during Trump's last two years in office.
Holding the announcement in the key battleground state of Georgia is seen as a strategic move to boost the fortunes of local Republican candidates.
Since he returned to the White House last year, Trump has used tariffs and political pressure to force global automakers to relocate their factories to American soil.
Audi's investment follows moves by Stellantis and Japan's Toyota to expand US production, while Honda is in talks to build a new US plant.
US auto giants General Motors and Ford have also promised to increase domestic production.
While one investment announcement may not be enough to sway many voters, it serves one of Trump's main election promises — to revive industrial production in the US.
Germany under pressure

articles.title: Brazil elections: Merz, world leaders congratulate Lula on his win
articles.summary: Brazilian President Lula secured a surprise win over far-right challenger Flavio Bolsonaro, who has refused to concede. DW has the latest.
articles.byline: Matt Ford, Akanksha Saxena, Richard Connor, Alex Berry

image.caption: Lula won a fourth term in the runoff despite having trailed Flavio Bolsonaro in the first round of votingImage: Raquel Cunha/REUTERS

blocks.text: October 26, 2026
Flavio Bolsonaro says he is banned from leaving Brazil after election defeat
Patrick Große

blocks.caption: Flavio Bolsonaro denies he has any plans to leave Brazil after his election defeat to Lula Image: Eraldo Peres/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro says he has been ordered to surrender his passports and is banned from leaving the country.
The right-wing senator said federal police approached him after he visited his imprisoned father, former President Jair Bolsonaro.
"I was ordered right on the street to hand over my passports, and I'm also prohibited from leaving the country," Bolsonaro said in a video posted on social media.

He called the move "a clear attempt to intimidate me" and claimed the order came from Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes. Neither the court nor federal police immediately confirmed the reported ruling.

Bolsonaro said the decision was based on comments by his brother Eduardo, who had suggested he should leave Brazil if he lost the election. He denied having any plans to flee the country and said he would comply with the order.

articles.title: UK sanctions Sudanese military leaders implicated in El Fasher ‘campaign of rape’
articles.summary:
Commanders suspected of sexual violence during the largest and fastest slaughter of civilians in more than 30 years have been subjected to travel ban and asset freeze

Senior Sudanese…

blocks.text: Senior Sudanese commanders implicated in a “campaign of rape” have been targeted by the UK on the first anniversary of a mass atrocity that saw tens of thousands of civilians killed over several days.

A year after the fall of El Fasher, the British government said it had sanctioned military leaders from both sides in the country’s ongoing conflict whom it suspected of sexual violence during the siege of the city.
A total of 15 commanders from the military groups – the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) – have been subjected to a travel ban and an asset freeze.
The Foreign Office said it hoped the action would ensure “the horrors that took place at El Fasher will be known to the world”.

During the RSF’s takeover of the city, up to 10,000 men, women and children are believed to have been slaughtered over two days – the fastest and largest massacre of civilians this century. Another 40,000 remain unaccounted for.
The killings came at the end of an 18-month starvation siege by the RSF, which was allegedly backed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The UAE continues to deny supporting the RSF.

Fewer than 70,000 people are believed to remain in El Fasher, compared with a prewar population of more than 1 million. Life inside the city continues to be horrendous, with testimony indicating routine detention, torture and unlawful killings.

Individuals targeted by the UK’s latest sanctions include Hussein Abu Jalak, an RSF colonel linked to atrocities during the siege, which forced hundreds of thousands of civilians to live off animal feed.
Another is Al-Nour Ahmed Adam – also known as “Al-Qubba” – who was identified as playing a prominent role in the attack on the city.
A Guardian investigation earlier this year revealed internal US and UK warnings were sidelined in the run-up to the RSF attack on El Fasher, and that action that might have saved lives was not taken.

A statement to mark the anniversary of the massacre from the Coalition on Atrocity Prevention and Justice for Sudan said: “The victims will not be forgotten, survivors will be heard, and we will continue to pursue accountability for those responsible.”
During the 12 months since the fall of El Fasher, Sudan’s ruinous conflict – which has forced 14 million people to flee their homes – has developed increasingly into a drone war.
The latest strikes saw the RSF causing mass power outages across east Sudan after targeting power stations with a coordinated drone attack.

articles.title: Japanese prosecutors charge US marine suspected of robbing and killing woman
articles.summary:
Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, denies charges that he fatally strangled Anna Yagi, 39, in a hotel on the island of Okinawa

Prosecutors in

blocks.text: Prosecutors in Japan have filed formal charges against a US marine suspected of murdering and robbing a woman while stationed on the country’s island of Okinawa, according to Japanese media.

Devin Jacob Ballard, a 20-year-old lance corporal assigned to Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in Okinawa, is charged with fatally strangling Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in the city and stealing from her a backpack containing a wallet, the public broadcaster NHK reported.

Ballard had initially been arrested in Yagi’s killing on 4 October, about a day after she was found dead in Naha, Okinawa’s capital. Prosecutors indicted him in the case on Sunday, and he has reportedly denied the charges.

NHK and other Japanese media outlets had previously reported that Ballard was arrested after surveillance camera footage from near the scene of Yagi’s killing showed a man entering a room with a woman and later leaving the scene with her belongings.
Ballard evidently matched the description of the suspect seen in the footage, was confronted and agreed to accompany investigators voluntarily to a local police station, Japanese media reported.

While being questioned by police, Ballard denied having a hand in Yagi’s killing, saying, “I don’t know anything about it,” NHK reported. But during subsequent questioning Ballard was alleged to have “made statements that partially hinted at his involvement”, the broadcaster reported.
A statement reported by NHK and reported to Yagi’s family on Sunday expressed a hope that Ballard “will confront what he has done and make amends commensurate with what he has done”.
“She lost her life at the young age of 39,” the statement from Yagi’s family added. “She … wanted to live much, much longer.”

Yagi’s killing prompted protests in Okinawa and the Japanese capital of Tokyo, with political leaders publicly condemning her killing. It also triggered a curfew and alcohol ban for US military members stationed in Okinawa, where most of the 54,000 US troops in Japan are based.
Crimes committed by US troops in Japan – including rape, assault, hit-and-run and drunk-driving – have long strained relations between the countries, which are close military allies.
A Japanese court in June 2025 sentenced US marine Jamel Clayton, then 22, to seven years in prison after he was convicted of choking and sexually assaulting a woman in her 20s.
In 2017, a former US marine and civilian military base worker named Kenneth Shinzato was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local Okinawa woman.
US military forces in Japan that same year banned all personnel from consuming alcohol after an intoxicated US marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing a local driver, age 61.
The Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper reported that about 6,000 US military personnel have been arrested since the US returned Okinawa to Japan after the second world war in 1972.
There were 80 such arrests in 2024, constituting a 20-year high.

After Ballard’s arrest, Shinjiro Koizumi, Japan’s defense minister, said: “Incidents and accidents involving US military personnel cause great anxiety among the local community and must not be allowed to happen.”
Reuters and Agence France-Presse contributed reporting

articles.title: Steinmeier in China: A major state visit in uncertain times
articles.summary: President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is traveling to China on a state visit in a period of political and economic uncertainty. Germany is seeking alternative partners in the region, but also wants good…

image.caption: Steinmeier begins a five-day trip to China on MondayImage: Hendrik Schmidt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Eight years have passed since Frank-Walter Steinmeier's last trip to China. Since then, the relationship between China and Europe has changed significantly. The German president plans to spend several days touring China before concluding his visit in Beijing, where he will meet with China's leaders.
His visit comes just as the Chinese Communist Party's Central Committee is convening for its plenary session, a major annual event that foreign dignitaries usually avoid when timing their visits.

The focus of the president's five-day trip will be "Germany's diverse and complex relations with China, as well as the challenges involved," his office said in a statement. In addition to sites of cultural exchange, the itinerary will also include a visit to a Volkswagen plant in Hefei.
A diplomatic balancing act

The automotive industry, in particular, illustrates the dilemma facing Germany's China policy. China is one of the most important markets for German automotive and machinery manufacturers, as well as for the chemical industry. At the same time, state-supported overcapacity in China is putting pressure on European manufacturers.
Not only that. Germany and Europe are dependent on China for raw materials and technologies, which means they are increasingly seeking out alternative partnerships.

Steinmeier was once an advocate of the policy of "change through trade" — the idea that other countries could be persuaded to become more democratic with the leverage of global trade — which has few adherents left in Germany today.

Now he must now pursue a tougher European line in Beijing. Caught between partnership and competition, Europe leaders recently managed to reach an agreement: Imports of plug-in hybrid vehicles from China are to be scaled back.
"That was a concrete step, but it can only be the beginning," said Michael Laha, an expert on China at the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP) in Berlin.
Why big automakers are losing China
Chancellor and president both in Asia

Coinciding with Steinmeier's state visit to China, Chancellor Friedrich Merz is traveling to the Indo-Pacific with business representatives. His visit to Japan, Singapore and South Korea will focus on competitiveness, technological upheavals, defense cooperation and critical raw materials. Merz is visiting companies and attending important regional economic conferences in Tokyo and Seoul.

The dual trips are Berlin's attempt to send a twofold message: While the chancellor is "deliberately strengthening Germany's partnerships in the Indo-Pacific at a time of global upheaval," according to Laha, the president is seeking dialogue with Beijing at a time when Germany and Europe are recalibrating their relationship with China.

"This joint trip sends a very well-coordinated message to the Chinese that we remain committed to the partnership but at the same time are taking steps to reduce risk," said Laha, before adding that this is a difficult balancing act that also allows China to save face.

blocks.caption: Steinmeier and Merz are traveling to Asia at the same timeImage: Markus Schreiber/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Little room for human rights

While Merz will be accompanied by a large economic delegation, Steinmeier will be traveling to China with representatives from German culture, politics, and academia. Mikko Huotari, director of the China Institute MERICS, is also expected to be part of the delegation — even though Beijing has imposed sanctions on the institute. "The fact that he is coming along sends a clear message to the Chinese side that we do not approve of the sanctions," said Laha.

In 2021, the EU imposed sanctions against several Chinese party and regional officials, as well as an organization accused of serious human rights violations and oppressing the Uyghur minority. It was the first time such sanctions had been imposed on China since the Tiananmen Square massacre in 1989, and Beijing did not take kindly to them:
. In response, the Chinese government imposed entry bans and other sanctions against European politicians, scholars, and institutions, including MERICS.

Laha did not expect human rights to play a major role in the German president's trip. Steinmeier is considered a pragmatist when it comes to China policy. As foreign minister, he distanced himself from his predecessor Joschka Fischer, a critic of China, and even criticized Chancellor Angela Merkel when she hosted the Dalai Lama.

blocks.caption: China's Xi Jinping is seeking greater influence in international affairsImage: Florence Lo/Reuters/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: China should assume international responsibility

On the subject of Ukraine, Steinmeier is likely to be more direct and raise the issue of China's role in the conflict. "Beijing is clearly on Moscow's side," said Laha. In Berlin, however, officials are convinced that China can do more to persuade Russia to engage in serious negotiations and find a solution to the conflict.

Steinmeier may make this clear in his speech at Peking University on Thursday. Germany has "long viewed China's emergence with respect and goodwill," read a statement from the president's office. Today, however, the focus is less on China's continued rise and more on how it uses its growing power.

"If the president points out that Russia used its power to attack a sovereign state, he could be alluding to another regional connection: Taiwan," said Laha. That could be seen as an appeal to Beijing to assume more responsibility for the regional and international order.

To conclude his visit, Steinmeier will meet with China's leadership in Beijing. Talks are planned with President Xi Jinping, whom he has known for nearly two decades, as well as with Premier Li Qiang and the chairman of the National People's Congress, Zhao Leji.

The trip marks the culmination of Steinmeier's focus on Asia during his second term in office. Since then, he has deliberately sought to forge close ties with partners in the region and has advocated for greater diversification. Now China – Germany's most important and most challenging partner – will come to its own conclusion.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Olivia Chow romps to victory as head of progressive new Toronto council

blocks.text: Toronto·Analysis

Olivia Chow will continue in the mayor's chair for another four years, after beating Brad Bradford. Chow won some 530,000 votes in an election where several of her key progressive allies also triumphed.
Ex-Liberal MP Nate Erskine-Smith and Chow's stepson Mike Layton also elected
Olivia Chow re-elected as Toronto mayor
Olivia Chow is preparing to lead Toronto for another four years, after an emphatic victory over former councillor Brad Bradford Monday night.
Chow will oversee a progressive, new-look council with several of her key allies elected, putting her in a strong position to pursue her agenda.
The returning mayor started the year looking comfortably ahead, before it appeared Bradford could surge into the mayor's chair.
In the end, she won a massive victory — netting roughly 530,000 votes, according to the unofficial results (official results will come once they've been certified by the city clerk).

items: GTA votes 2026: Catch up on everything you need to know from election night

blocks.text: A close race and new messaging
While Bradford received just one per cent of the vote in the 2023 mayoral byelection, he gained on Chow through 2026.
As the race heated up after Labour Day, the gap between challenger and incumbent appeared to narrow significantly.
The timing of the surge seemed like it would be good for Bradford, coming toward the end of the race, when advance voting appeared to be more than 70 per cent higher than the 2023 mayoral byelection.

But as polling suggested the wind was in Bradford's sails, the Chow campaign settled on a clear message about the challenger and his platform, particularly his pledge to create a public utility company to handle the city's water and wastewater.
Toronto mayoral candidates make final push ahead of election day

Bradford said the plan would help raise funds for city hall and cut costs for residents, but Chow said it would mean the city losing control of an asset that is working well and opens the door to privatization.
That message may have struck a nerve with Torontonians, said political strategist Blue Knox, who served as former mayor John Tory's director of communications.
"Canadians like for their public institutions to stay public," she said.
"Her campaign was able — whether you agree with it or not — to very clearly distill their attack on one of Brad Bradford's promises."
Olivia Chow, left, and Brad Bradford were the two front-runners to be Toronto's mayor in a race polls suggested was close at the end. (CBC)
Erin Morrison, vice president of Texture Communications and a Chow supporter, said she thought the policy was a "serious mistake" from the Bradford campaign.
"That really started to play a role in the campaign with about 10 days to go," she said.
"Chow, to her credit, really knew that that was problematic to her voters … and made an issue out of it."
Strong get-out-the-vote operation
The Chow campaign was able to rely on a formidable team to help spread her campaign message and her criticism of her opponent.
She ran a "disciplined campaign," Knox said.
Even the Bradford campaign acknowledged on election night the combination of Progress Toronto, Ontario NDP supporters and unions backing Chow was a formidable force to reckon with.
'I will work every day to earn your trust,' says Chow during victory speech
"It's tough organizationally," Bradford's head of communications Laryssa Waler said shortly before polls closed.
"They know how to get them out to vote. They have union support, they're very, very organized."
Mandate to stay on the same path
While Bradford's camp had offered a slew of new ideas, particularly around the city's finances, Chow's camp stayed close to her record: renters, transit fares and a school nutrition program.
Knox said the Chow campaign's decision to stick to a few key promises building on the work of her first term in office will make for a smoother transition.
It means Chow's "hands aren't tied" to a series of rigid campaign pledges and she will get to "be flexible to different circumstances that come up."
Bradford conceded to Chow on election night. (Prasanjeet Chaudhary/CBC)

Chow pledged a 10-ride fare cap for riders on the TTC, enhanced protections for renters, a school lunch program and tax cuts for independent grocers. She also said she would continue work to build more affordable housing.
Delivering those promises will be made easier by a council still relatively aligned with Chow's core goals.
A number of high-profile progressive allies, including Nate Erskine-Smith and Mike Layton, Chow's own stepson, will join her at city hall.
'The cost of living is a problem': Olivia Chow's pitch to Toronto (in her own words)
Morrison said the 2026-2030 council should be one Chow can lead on most issues — getting her agenda through without needing to resort to strong mayor powers, which she has said she will not use.
"I think that tonight is good news for Chow in the sense that she's got even more progressive allies on council," she said.
"I think she's going to find it an easy council to work with."

articles.title: Who is Lula? From ex-worker and prisoner to Brazil's president again
articles.summary: The firebrand left-winger, who has at times been at odds with Trump, has won his fourth term as Brazil's president.

blocks.text: Lula's first presidential victory in 2002 marked the end of an unprecedented journey from poverty.
The son of a poor, illiterate peasant family, Lula worked as a peanut seller and shoe-shine boy as a child, only learning to read when he was 10 years old.
He went on to train as a metalworker and found work in an industrial city near São Paulo, where he lost the little finger of his left hand in an accident in the 1960s.
Lula was not initially interested in politics, but threw himself into trade union activism.

Elected leader of the 100,000-strong Metalworkers' Union in 1975, he transformed trade union activism in Brazil by turning what had mostly been government-friendly organisations into a powerful independent movement.

In 1980, Lula brought together a combination of trade unionists, intellectuals, Trotskyites and Church activists to found the Workers' Party (PT), the first major socialist party in the country's history.
The PT went on to gradually replace its revolutionary commitment to changing the power structure in Brazil with a more pragmatic, social democratic platform.
Lula came to power promising major reforms to the country's political and economic system.
He vowed to eradicate hunger and create a self-confident, caring, outward-looking nation.
In his time in office, Lula pumped billions of dollars into social programmes and can reasonably claim to have helped reverse Brazil's historic inequalities.

By increasing the minimum wage well above the rate of inflation and broadening state help to the most impoverished with a family grant programme, the Bolsa Familia, he helped some 44 million people and cemented his support among the poor.
However, many commentators argue that the programme failed to address the structural problems that underpin poverty, such as a lack of education.

He left office eight years later, after serving two terms as president, enjoying exceptionally high popularity ratings for a retiring Latin American leader - 83% - having raised Brazil's profile on the international scene and presided over the longest period of economic growth in three decades.

Unable to run for a third term, Lula left the presidency and, shortly afterwards, was diagnosed with throat cancer. He even shaved his trademark beard during treatment. Doctors declared him cured of the disease in 2012.

Under his chosen successor, progress stalled. The economic boom also gave way to recession, and the country's political scene was rocked by a huge investigation into top-level corruption, known as Operation Car Wash.

Lula was among those to get caught up in the scandal. In July 2017, he was convicted of corruption and sentenced to more than nine years in prison for accepting a beachside flat as a bribe from engineering firm OAS - a sentence increased on appeal to 12 years.

Lula was also jailed for 12 years and 11 months for corruption and money laundering for receiving bribes from two construction and engineering firms by way of funding improvements in a country house he and his family used.
He has always maintained his innocence, insisting accusations against him were politically motivated.
In 2019, he was released after having served just over 18 months, after a Supreme Court ruling that the incarceration had been illegal, having come before all appeals had been exhausted.
Those convictions were annulled in 2021, leaving Lula free to run for a third term in 2022, beating right-winger Jair Bolsonaro.
When he re-entered office in 2023, he vowed it would be his last term, and yet his party endorsed him as their candidate again this year, even though he will turn 81 on Tuesday.
Even backers of the PT will acknowledge that he achieved more in his first two terms - from January 2003 to December 2010 - than in his most recent four years in office.

And while his supporters described him ahead of the 2022 election as the "saviour of the Amazon", praising his commitment to protecting the rainforest, some environmentalists have been critical of some of his recent actions.
His support for exploratory oil drilling in offshore waters near the mouth of the Amazon in particular has drawn criticism.
Lula insists that he remains committed to eventually phasing out fossil fuels and argues that oil revenues are key to financing Brazil's transition to clean energy.

His government has also pointed to the reduction in deforestation in the Amazon - satellite data suggests the area deforested in the first half of 2026 was reduced to its lowest in the past decade - as proof that its policies were working.
Lula's third term coincided with the return to office of Trump.
The two men represent different ends of the political spectrum and have found it impossible not to voice their differences in public.
The Brazilian leader told the BBC in September 2025 that he had no relationship with Trump.

Even though the US has a trade surplus with Brazil, Donald Trump imposed 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods in July that year, citing the trial on coup charges of Brazil's right-wing former president Jair Bolsonaro as a trigger. Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year jail sentence and it was his son, Flávio, who Lula beat in Sunday's election run-off.

Lula accused Trump of foreign interference and said "he's not emperor of the world". But their relationship improved after a White House in May this year, after which the two leaders exchanged public compliments - Trump called Lula "dynamic", while the Brazilian president said he left the meeting "very satisfied".
In July of this year, the US imposed 25% tariffs on most goods, external from Brazil.
The two governments still disagree on key issues such as crime, and Lula acknowledged they are especially far apart on trade.

Referring to what Trump has dubbed the "Donroe doctrine" - his administration's national security strategy which asserts that US dominance in the Western hemisphere should not be interfered with - Lula has insisted that "Brazil does not fit into anyone's backyard".

articles.title: Five ways Trump has changed immigration in the US
articles.summary: This is how his signature policy has played out after returning to power promising a closed border and mass deportations.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
ByBernd Debusmann Jr and Mike Hills
Immigration has always been central to Donald Trump's message.

When he famously stepped onto the golden escalator at Trump Tower to announce his candidacy for his first presidential term in 2015, he accused Mexico of sending drugs and crime north of the border - and it's been a constant rallying cry ever since.
Some of his first-term ambitions to stem the flow of would-be immigrants were constrained by the courts.
But restraints have been weaker in his second term, with a more accommodating Supreme Court and tens of billions of additional enforcement money from Congress.
Who should be allowed to live in the US remains a big issue on the minds of voters in the upcoming midterm elections, which are largely seen as a referendum on the Trump presidency.
He promised a closed border and mass deportations in his successful 2024 campaign - and few can deny that he's delivered on both.
But even among those who voted for a tougher stance, there is a concern that the crackdown has gone too far.
His signature policy has played out in five key ways.
1. A border that is largely closed

Crossings exploded during Joe Biden's presidency, with over 4.5 million migrant "encounters" recorded at the southern border in 2023 and 2024 alone, reflecting the massive numbers of people headed north to the US border.
His administration eventually brought the monthly figures down significantly by restricting asylum claims and removing migrants entering the US illegally without processing.
When Trump returned to office, that stream of migrants became a trickle. Border encounters plummeted.
By the end of Trump's first year in office, the chaotic scenes that had generated headlines around the globe during the Biden administration had largely gone.

On a trip to the border city of El Paso, Texas, in November 2025, for example, the BBC found quiet streets where there had previously been makeshift camps housing thousands of migrants granted parole in the US to await immigration proceedings.

blocks.caption: Bar chart showing the numbers detained at the southern US border since 2017. The red bars denote Trump's first term and his second term so far. The blue bars show Biden's term. The chart shows numbers peaked midway in Trump's first term at about 140,000 a month but came down again before starting…

blocks.text: To achieve what he often describes as the "most secure" border in US history, the Trump administration has taken an aggressive, multi-pronged approach.

That has included effectively freezing asylum applications at the border, ending "catch and release" of detainees into the US, deploying troops to the border and pressuring Mexico to clamp down on the flow of migrants headed north.
"President Trump promised the American people a secure border, and the data proves he delivered," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement on 16 October.
"The results could not be clearer: strong enforcement works."
2. Building of wall speeding up
A vow to build a "big, beautiful wall" at the nearly 2,000-mile (3,218km) US-Mexico border was a signature promise of Trump's 2016 campaign.
Progress on it has speeded up in his second term, boosted by $46.5bn (£34.7bn) in new funding from Trump's "One Big Beautiful" spending bill.

According to government figures, external, about 644 miles of "primary wall" - closest to the border - existed before Trump returned to the White House, in addition to 75 miles of "secondary" wall set slightly further inside the US.

Since then, 250 more miles of new wall have been completed, including primary, secondary and waterborne barriers, along with the technology that helps detect illegal crossings. An additional 1,443 miles of barriers are currently under construction.
Experts, however, paint a more complex picture of what has been actually built rather than just improved or updated.
Additionally, the impact the wall is itself having on the broader immigration figures is up for debate.

blocks.caption: Map of the US-Mexico border showing existing border barriers and planned construction work as of October 2026. Grey lines mark barriers that were already in place before President Trump's second term. Red sections, labelled "being built", make up most of the new construction and are concentrated…

blocks.text: "Since new wall construction has really begun in earnest, there has been no significant change in the number of people crossing the border," said Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, an immigration enforcement expert at the American Immigration Council.
There is no indication the border wall has reduced migrant crossings, he added. The reduction has been more down to Trump's policies and messaging.
Trump, for his part, continues to point to the wall as a successful policy - and continues to claim that Mexico paid for it.

"I'm the King of the Wall," Trump said at a rally in Kentucky on 17 October. "By the way, Mexico did pay for that wall. I charged them tariffs and I charged them costs like they've never paid in history."
3. Detentions and deportations rocketing

Most of the headlines generated by Trump's immigration policies have come from the US interior, where operations by Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents to round up people they say are in the US illegally have rocked cities across the country.

During his campaign, Trump promised an immediate start to what he described as the "largest deportation operation in American history", which officials said would begin with people who have committed crimes first.

Arrests - and subsequent detentions in immigration facilities - have shot up significantly since Trump returned to office, including a record of nearly 50,000 in July this year alone, according to data obtained by the Deportation Data Project, external, a repository of US immigration data run out of University of California, Berkeley, and UCLA.

But the same data, external shows that a large chunk of the arrests involve people without criminal convictions. In July 2026, detentions of immigrants with criminal histories reached an all-time low of 27%.

Deportations have also ramped up significantly. By mid-July this year, ICE was removing an average of 1,255 people from the country per day, compared to about 770 in Biden's final months in office - although Biden's own removals had sharply risen in his final year in office.

blocks.caption: Monthly bar chart of people detained by ICE for the first time between 2019 and 2026. Arrests were generally around 10,000 to 12,000 a month during Trump's first term before falling in 2020. Under Biden, arrests gradually rose from around 2,000 a month in early 2021 to about 8,000 by late 2024. A…

blocks.text: But the tactics used by ICE in US cities have made many Americans grow uncomfortable, including many of those who supported stricter restrictions broadly. This became increasingly evident following Operation Metro Surge, a two-month large scale enforcement action in Minneapolis in early 2026 that left two US citizens dead.

A New York Times and Siena poll, external released on 21 October found that 50% of voters trust Democrats to handle the issue, compared with 46% for Republicans - despite the issue being a traditional Republican strength.

A separate poll, from Politico and Public First, external in late September, found deep splits between Republicans on the issue, with 31% of non-MAGA Republicans, meaning those not aligned with Trump's movement, believing that campaign has become too aggressive.
Watch: Texas voters share concerns over cost of living ahead of midterms
4. Refugee intake down sharply
After returning to the White House last year, Trump almost immediately suspended refugee admissions, saying at the time these could only restart if they were shown to be in US interests.

In February, however, an executive order signed by Trump narrowly re-opened that process for Afrikaners from South Africa, who the White House has repeatedly said are being killed and "persecuted" - a claim that the government in Pretoria has denied.

The cap for refugee admissions for the 2026 fiscal year was initially set at 7,500, which was raised to 17,500 in May this year because of what the administration described as an "unforeseen emergency refugee situation".
Overall refugee admissions have slowed to a relative trickle. State Department data shows that 16,292 refugees were admitted into the US in the 2026 fiscal year - of whom 16,287 were South African.

blocks.caption: Bar chart showing annual refugee admissions to the US from 2017 to 2026. Admissions fell sharply during Donald Trump’s first term, dropping from about 53,000 in 2017 to around 12,000 in 2020. Under Joe Biden, admissions increased each year, reaching about 100,000 in 2024. After Trump returned to…

blocks.text: By comparison, in the final two fiscal years of the Biden administration - 2023 and 2024 - 60,000 and 100,000 entered the country, respectively. In the 2024 fiscal year, the highest numbers came from Democratic Republic of Congo, Afghanistan, Syria and Venezuela.

Hundreds of thousands of people protected from deportation lost that protection when a humanitarian protection called Temporary Protected Status (TPS) was also ended in Trump's second term. It gave vetted individuals the right to live and work in the US if their home countries were deemed to be unsafe to return to.
One of those countries was Haiti. In June, the Supreme Court upheld the Trump administration's decision to end TPS for some 350,000 Haitians in the US.
5. A squeeze on visas - and a $1m golden ticket
Other legal pathways to come to live and work in the US have also been tightened up, through various policy changes.
Dozens of countries the Trump administration has deemed a security risk have been subject to a full or partial freeze on visas and travel.
Enhanced vetting and new rules that send people residing in the US back to their home countries to apply for green cards has slowed that process down.

And in September 2025, a $100,000 fee on new H1-B visas for skilled workers, mostly held by Indians, stunned the US tech industry. In May this year, the US Citizenship and Immigration Services said on X, external that registrations for 2027 were down 40%.

"The data is a clear sign that the days of abusing the program with mass, low-wage registrations are over, and that the program is better serving its intended purpose of attracting highly skilled foreign workers and protecting the wages, working conditions and job opportunities of American workers," the statement added.

While a court has blocked the $100,000 fee - for now - the threat of it appears to have deterred employers. But some experts have cautioned the administration's aim of protecting American jobs, raising wages and stopping firms from outsourcing may prove elusive.

One study, from the Wharton School of Business, external, found that the H1-B changes would have "no significant impact" on the wages of US-born workers, with any reduction in competition offset by reduced productivity growth.

blocks.caption: Bar chart showing annual H1-B visa registrations from fiscal years 2021 to 2026. During the Biden administration, registrations rose from about 275,000 in 2021 to nearly 800,000 in 2024. Registrations then declined, with fiscal year 2025 at about 480,000 and fiscal year 2026 at around 360,000 aft…

blocks.text: Other pathways to the US have been opened, however - if you have a spare million.
The "Trump Gold Card" launched in 2025 sought to entice wealthy foreigners to come live in the US in exchange for a $1m "gift" to the US government, plus a non-refundable $15,000 application fee.
At the time, Trump said that the programme would boost the US economy. Its uptake, however, appears to be minimal so far. By April, only one applicant had been accepted.

articles.title: US forces accused of ‘weaponising’ Somalia’s floods by trapping women and children in the path of El Niño
articles.summary: Exclusive: Coordinated airstrikes on territory held by al-Shabaab are driving the civilian population to find refuge alongside a river where rising water levels are a threat to…

blocks.text: The water was rising rapidly. It had already reached Cayni Ali’s waist. Her home, five metres from the flooded River Juba in southern Somalia, never stood a chance. There was nowhere to go. Ali’s city of Jilib was under attack. Repeated airstrikes, said the mother of six, were pinning its population beside the rising river.
“The drones come all the time,” said the 27-year-old. “We hear them constantly. They kill animals, civilians. The town is big but destruction is everywhere.”

blocks.caption: Cayni Ali with her child Mandeq at a health centre in Kismayo, Somalia.  Photograph: Hugh Kinsella Cunningham

blocks.text: Asho Omar from Malenda, a village near Jilib, described “constant” airstrikes that had forced people towards the banks of the Juba.
“The airstrikes are everywhere; it is difficult to move. So many people have been killed.”

Their testimony offers a rare glimpse of life inside the stronghold of al-Shabaab, the Islamist militants who control 30% of Somalia. Closed off from the outside world, residents describe a city dealing with significant civilian casualties. Bodies, some said, lay in the streets.
The ongoing conflict is a legally ambiguous, shadowy war coordinated by the United States in east Africa, in which there is little accountability for harm to Somali civilians.

The United States Africa Command (Africom) would not share “operational security” details of a seemingly accelerating campaign that has also raised questions over potential covert US strikes. But there is, perhaps, an even darker dimension to the offensive on al-Shabaab’s de facto capital.

Sources say the military strategy appears to be seeking to drown those living in al-Shabaab territory by “weaponising” a rapidly strengthening El Niño, forecast to intensify Somalia’s rainy season from this month.

blocks.caption: An aerial view of the Juba River, close to the town of Kismayo.  Photograph: Hugh Kinsella Cunningham

blocks.text: “The airstrikes are forcing people to go close to the river. It’s an extremely aggressive offensive, exploiting El Niño as a weapon of war to push the population into flood-prone areas,” said a source monitoring the Juba floodplain in southern Somalia.
Pinning the population – which includes large numbers of women and children – on the river’s floodplain has raised concerns of large-scale deaths in the months ahead.
“The official line is that they are targeting military positions and al-Shabaab, but because al-Shabaab is embedded within the community, it’s difficult to avoid collateral damage,” added the source.

When El Niño last struck Somalia in 2023, it caused the worst floods seen in the country for a century, displacing more than 1.2 million people. Analysts have questioned the ethics of the US military allegedly using mapping data from flood-prone areas – conceived to mitigate civilian casualties – to inflict harm.

Jethro Norman, a senior researcher with the Danish Institute for International Studies, said: “A weaponisation of El Niño is a reversal of process – using humanitarian remote sensing to inflict casualties rather than to mitigate harm. You capture the cumulative impact of a sustained airstrikes campaign in an El Niño flooding context.”

blocks.caption: The aftermath of the 2023 El Niño in Luuq district, Jubaland, which caused the worst floods ever seen in the country.  Photograph: Feisal Omar/Reuters

blocks.text: US officials deny exploiting climatic factors. A spokesperson said: “Africom does not target civilians, conduct operations for the purpose of displacing civilian populations or use weather or flooding as a method of warfare. Africom targets lawful military objectives and takes feasible measures to mitigate civilian harm.”
Nevertheless, many wonder if the opportunity to weaken al-Shabaab using the weather was too tempting to ignore, offering a catastrophic drowning event blamed on a supercharged El Niño.

Like many cities, Jilib’s location has been found wanting in an era of extreme weather. On a low-lying plain, the city is chronically vulnerable to flooding. In 2023, vast swathes of farmland were submerged. Halimo Abdikadir from Kamsuuma, south of Jillib, described the destruction of her home, 6 miles (10km) from the river. “The waters came quickly at night – when they left, everything was mud. A lot of animals drowned.”
Arbey Famu from Ahmed Yare, another village outside Jilib, expects this El Niño to be far worse than 2023: her crops of maize and sorghum are underwater.
